en: The Noble *Saṃghāṭa Sūtra*.
(May there be well-being! Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!

<1> Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain together with a great saṅgha of monks, with twenty-two thousand monks, such as the venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya. <2>
And with the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
and with the venerable Śāradvatīputra;
and with the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
And with the venerable Rāhula;
and with the venerable Bakkula;
and with the venerable Bhadrāvāsya.
And with the venerable Bhadraśrī,
and with the venerable Nandaśrī,
and with the venerable Jāṅguli.
And with the venerable Subhūti,
and the venerable Revata,
and the venerable Nandasena.
Together with the Venerable Ānanda,
twenty-two thousand bhikṣus headed by him,
and sixty-two thousand bodhisattvas, such as the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya.
and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sarvaśūra;
and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Kumāraśrī;
and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Kumāravāsin.
and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Kumārabhadra; and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Anūna.
And with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta; and with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra;
and with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sudarśana.
And with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja,
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrasena—
headed by these sixty-two thousand Bodhisattvas.
And with sixty-two thousand sons of gods, such as the son of god Arjuna,
the son of god Bhadra,
and the son of god Subhadra.
And by the divine son Dharmaruci,
and by the divine son Candanagarbha,
and by the divine son Candavāsin.
And by the divine son Candana,
and by the divine son Candanasena—
headed by these, there were sixty-two thousand divine sons.
And with eight thousand celestial maidens, such as the celestial maiden Mṛdaṅginī,
the celestial maiden Prāsādavatī,
and the celestial maiden Mahātmasaṃprayuktā.
And of the divine maiden Varṣaśrī,
and of the divine maiden Padmaśrī,
and of the divine maiden Prajāpativāsinī.
And with the divine maiden Balinī,
and with the divine maiden Subāhuyuktā—
thus led by these eight thousand divine maidens.
And with eight thousand nāga kings, namely: the nāga king Apalāla,
the nāga king Elapatra,
and the nāga king Timiṅgila.
And by the nāga king Kumbhasāra;
and by the nāga king Kumbhaśīrṣa;
and by the nāga king Sunanda.
And by the nāga king Suśākha,
and by the nāga king Gavaśīrṣa—
by these eight thousand nāga kings, headed by such as these.

They all went toward the great city of Rājagṛha, toward Vulture Peak Mountain, and toward the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha; having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and stood before him.

They said this: “May the Blessed One teach the Dharma; may the Sugata teach the Dharma, hearing which we might quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and by which the karmic obstructions of all sentient beings might be exhausted. And the Blessed One consented by remaining silent.

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, many tens of millions of gods, tens of millions of celestial nymphs, and tens of millions of Bodhisattvas, as well as many tens of millions of Śrāvakas, have gathered and are seated here to hear the Dharma."

Therefore, O Blessed One, it would be well if the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, were to teach such an entrance into the method of Dharma to those who have thus assembled (and are seated),

so that it may be for their long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness, as well as for that of gods and humans; and by means of such an entrance into the method of Dharma being taught, [there may be] for the elder beings...

By the mere hearing [of this], all their karmic obscurations would go to complete exhaustion; and young beings, applying themselves to wholesome qualities, would attain distinction, and would neither decline nor fall away from wholesome qualities.

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra: "Excellent, excellent, Sarvaśūra! It is indeed excellent, Sarvaśūra, that you consider it necessary to ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, about this matter.
Therefore, Sarvaśūra, listen well and attend closely to what I shall say to you."
“‘So be it, Blessed One,’ the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then said this to him: ‘Sarvaśūra, there is a discourse on the Dharma (*saddharmaparyāya*), by means of which discourse on the Dharma the fivefold karmic obstructions of immediate retribution for all sentient beings are brought to exhaustion...’”
In this way, other karmic obscurations are also brought to exhaustion, and they swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. "Blessed One, what is that discourse on the true Dharma?
The Blessed One said:
The Dharma discourse named Saṃghāṭa,
which shall now circulate in Jambudvīpa—
whosoever, O Sarvaśūra, shall hear this Saṃghāṭa Dharma discourse.

His five deeds of immediate retribution will be completely exhausted, and he shall become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. <15> What do you think, Sarvaśūra? Regarding one who hears this Dharma discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*?
"Just as the mass of merit from honoring a single Tathāgata, so much of a mass of merit will that being produce.
"It should not be viewed in this way, Sarvaśūra," he said.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra then asked:
"But how, Blessed One, should it be viewed?
The Blessed One said:
"Just as if one were to perform acts of honor toward Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā."

Sarvaśūra, those beings will produce a mass of merit as great as that; Sarvaśūra, all those who hear this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa* shall become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
and they shall all behold the Tathāgata.
And all shall behold the Tathāgatas; and all shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
and they shall be invincible to Māra, the Evil One.
And all those who, O Sarvaśūra, shall hear this Saṃghāṭa Sūtra will attain that very same wholesome dharma;
they shall all know arising and cessation.

Then, at that time and on that occasion, all those [bodhisattvas, great śrāvakas] who had gathered there, as well as millions of gods, nāgas, humans, and apsarases, rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, placed their right knees upon the ground,
and extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One. All of them—
They questioned the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, how great is the mass of merit for one who has performed an act of veneration toward a single Tathāgata?"
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, son of good family!

The measure of the mass of merit of a single Buddha is like this: it is like the drops of water in the great ocean, as many as the atoms in Jambudvīpa, or equal to the sentient beings who are like the sands of the river Gaṅgā."
Suppose all those beings were to become bodhisattvas established on the ten stages; the mass of merit belonging to those bodhisattvas would be far surpassed by the mass of merit of a single Buddha.

And yet, O Sarvaśūra, those beings who hear this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa* will produce an even greater mass of merit than that—it is impossible to reach the limit of that mass of merit through the application of calculation.
Sarvaśūra, when at that time and on that occasion they hear these words, they will experience great enthusiasm and will produce such an immeasurable mass of merit.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, who are those beings who will be thirsty for the Dharma?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra: "Sarvaśūra, there are these two kinds of beings who are thirsty for the Dharma."

"Which two? That is to say, Sarvaśūra, one who possesses a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; and second, Sarvaśūra, one who, having heard the Dharma, proclaims it equally to all sentient beings. These two are those who thirst for the Dharma. The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra asked: "Blessed One, what is that Dharma which, having been heard, is proclaimed equally to all sentient beings?"
The Blessed One said: "Sarvaśūra, one person, having heard the Dharma, dedicates it toward awakening.
And when one dedicates it toward awakening, then all sentient beings will become thirsty for the Dharma.
Sarvaśūra, the second person is he who plunges into the Mahāyāna; he is constantly thirsty for the Dharma."

<21> Then those tens of millions of gods, nāgas, humans, and apsarases rose from their seats, joined their palms in reverence before the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, we are parched with thirst for the Dharma;
may the Blessed One fulfill our aspirations and those of all sentient beings.
<22> Then, at that moment, the Blessed One manifested a smile. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat and extended his joined palms toward where the Blessed One was.
Having bowed down to the Blessed One, he said this: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for manifesting this smile?
Then the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra:
"Sarvaśūra, those beings who come here, they all attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
All of them attain perfection for the sake of perfecting the domain of the Tathāgata.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, that these beings, having come here, realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, Sarvaśūra, that you consider it necessary to ask the Tathāgata about this matter."
Therefore, Sarvaśūra, listen!
Here, Sarvaśūra, a distinction in dedication is to be seen.
Once upon a time, Sarvaśūra, in the past, incalculable eons ago, at that time and at that moment, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Ratnaśrī.
There arose one endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, at that time I was a young brahmin; and those beings who are now established by me in the knowledge of a Buddha, all of them at that time and on that occasion—

At that time and on that occasion, I made this vow: "May all those deer who are currently tormented by suffering be reborn in my buddha-field, and may I establish them all in the knowledge of a Buddha. When those deer heard those words, they spoke these words: "So be it!
Sarvaśūra, by virtue of that root of merit, these beings, having come here, will realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra, having heard that encouragement from the presence of the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what will be the measure of the lifespan of those beings?
The Blessed One said:
"The lifespan of those beings will be eighty-four thousand kalpas.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra asked, "Blessed One, what is the measure of a kalpa?
The Blessed One said, "Listen, son of good family."

Sarvaśūra, it is as if, for example, some man were to build a city twelve yojanas in length and breadth, with a height of three yojanas; and that man were to fill that city completely with sesame seeds. Suppose that man lived by the hair of his head [and subsisted on a single hair each day]. Then, after the passing of a hundred years, that man were to take a single sesame seed from that city filled with sesame seeds and cast it outside. In this manner, that man would [eventually] exhaust all of those...
He would cause the sesame seeds to perish and bring them to total exhaustion; yet that city would remain without root or foundation, and even now the eon would not have been exhausted.
Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, I shall provide another analogy for the sake of establishing this very point.
Suppose there were a mountain measuring twenty-five *yojanas* in breadth and twelve *yojanas* in height.
Then, suppose a certain man were to build a house on the side of that mountain and, after the lapse of a hundred years of a long duration, were to wipe it once with a cloth from Kāśī. In this manner—
Even if that mountain were to be exhausted, the eon would not be exhausted.
This, Sarvaśūra, is the measure of an eon.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and [proceeded] toward...
He said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, by means of a single dedication, one produces such a vast mass of merit that for eighty eons the measure of one's lifespan will be happiness.
What need is there to mention one who will perform even greater service within the teaching of the Tathāgata?"
"What will be the measure of his lifespan?
The Blessed One said, "Listen, son of good family: whoever hears this *Saṃghāṭa* Sūtra, the measure of his lifespan will be eighty-four thousand eons."
How much more so, Sarvaśūra, for one who will cause the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* to be written down or recited; that being will produce a far greater mass of merit.
Sarvaśūra, whoever, with a clear mind and through resolute intention, pays homage to the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, shall remember their past births for ninety-five eons.
For sixty thousand eons he will be a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
Sarvaśūra, in this very life, he will be dear and pleasing to all. Sarvaśūra, he shall not meet his end by means of weapons;
Sarvaśūra, he will be dear and pleasing, and he shall not meet his end by means of weapons.
He shall not meet his end by poison (nor by water, nor by fire);
and no *kākhorda* sorcery shall overcome him.
At the time of death, when the final cessation is occurring, he will behold ninety million Buddhas face to face.

And all those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, O Sarvaśūra, will comfort him, saying: "Do not fear, noble son! By you, having heard this well-spoken *Saṃghāṭa* Sūtra, this great Dharma-discourse, such a mass of merit has been produced. To those ninety-five million Buddhas...

In each and every world-system, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will grant predictions. How much more so, Sarvaśūra, for one who hears this *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, this great Dharma-discourse, in its entirety and in detail—
whether they write it down, recite it, or cultivate it?
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, I shall hear the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, the great Dharma-discourse.
Blessed One, how much of a mass of merit shall I produce?”

The Blessed One said: "Sarvaśūra, that being shall produce a mass of merit equal to the mass of merit produced by honoring as many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said: "Blessed One, as I listen to this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, I do not know satiety, O Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Sarvaśūra! You do not conceive of satiety regarding the teachings.
I too, Sarvaśūra, do not conceive of satiety regarding the teachings;
how much less, Sarvaśūra, could foolish ordinary people conceive of satiety?"
<34> Any noble son or noble daughter, Sarvaśūra, who shall produce faith in the Mahāyāna will not go to a state of ruin for a thousand eons;
for five thousand eons they will not be reborn among animals.
For twelve thousand kalpas he will possess evil intelligence;
for eighteen thousand kalpas he will not be reborn in a border region;
and for twenty thousand kalpas he will be a hero in giving.
For twenty-five thousand kalpas he will be reborn in the world of the gods;
for thirty-five thousand kalpas he will practice celibacy;
and for forty thousand kalpas he will live as one who has gone forth from the household life.
For fifty thousand kalpas he will be a bearer of the Dharma;
for sixty-five thousand kalpas he will cultivate the recollection of death.
For that noble son or noble daughter, Sarvaśūra, no evil karmas whatsoever shall be experienced.
Moreover, Māra the Evil One shall find no opportunity to harm them;
they shall never again be reborn in a mother’s womb—
those, Sarvaśūra, who hear this Saṃghāṭa Dharma-discourse.
Wherever they shall be reborn, there for ninety-five incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) they shall not fall into the lower realms.
For eighty thousand eons they shall be retainers of what they have heard (*śrutadhara*).
For a hundred thousand eons they shall abstain from taking life. For ninety-nine thousand eons they shall abstain from false speech.
For thirteen thousand eons, they will be free from malicious speech.
Sarvaśūra, those beings who shall hear this Dharma-discourse are rare to find.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One.
Having bowed down to the Blessed One, he said this: "Blessed One, how great will be the mass of demerit produced by those beings who shall reject this Dharma-discourse?"

The Blessed One said: "Sarvaśūra, one will produce a vast heap of demerit from the rejection of the true Dharma. Sarvaśūra asked: "Blessed One, how great will be the heap of evil karma for those beings?

The Blessed One said: "Enough, enough, Sarvaśūra! Do not ask me about that heap of evil karma. Nevertheless, Sarvaśūra, listen; I shall explain to you the evil [karma] of those who reject the true Dharma."
The mass of unwholesome [karma];
as much of that evil, unwholesome mass as they shall take upon themselves,
who reject this Dharma-exposition.

And, Sarvaśūra, whoever should give rise to a malicious mind toward as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are grains of sand in twelve Ganges rivers, and whoever should reject this Saṃghāṭa Sūtra—
this latter person will produce far more demerit than the former. (From this, O Sarvaśūra, a mass of merit will arise.)
They will produce a mass of unwholesome karma.
Therefore, Sarvaśūra, those beings who reject the true Dharma and give rise to a mind of malice toward the Mahāyāna will produce a much greater mass of unwholesome karma.
Sarvaśūra, those beings are burnt; they are truly burnt.
Sarvaśūra said: “Blessed One, those beings cannot be liberated.
The Blessed One said: “Listen, Sarvaśūra; they cannot be liberated.”

Sarvaśūra, it is just as if some man were to cut off the head of a certain being, and then that man were to smear that head with some medicine, or with honey, or sugar, or molasses, or ghee, or oil. What do you think, Sarvaśūra? Would it be possible for that being to be raised up again?
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said: "It is not possible, Blessed One; it is not possible, Sugata.
The Blessed One said: "In this very way, Sarvaśūra, it is not possible to liberate that being by means of many expedients who has conceived a mind of malice toward the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Sarvaśūra:

It is just as if there were a second person who, with a sharp weapon, should strike another being; although he might not be able to deprive him of life with a single blow, nevertheless, O Sarvaśūra, a wound would be produced.
Yet, if one then applies medicinal treatment, then he is freed from the wound.
When he is completely liberated, he then remembers his suffering and thinks:
"I now understand; I shall never again perform the formative action of sinful and unwholesome karma.
In this very way, Sarvaśūra, when that person who has rejected the true Dharma remembers the suffering in hell, he then completely abandons all evil.
When one completely abandons all evil,
then one will bring all phenomena before oneself;
having brought all phenomena before oneself, then...
He will bring all wholesome dharmas to full completion.

Sarvaśūra, it is just as when the parents of a deceased man grieve and lament, yet they are unable to save him; in the very same way, Sarvaśūra, foolish ordinary beings are unable to accomplish their own welfare or the welfare of others, being like parents who have come to despair.
In the same way, Sarvaśūra, those beings become hopeless at the time of death.
Sarvaśūra, there are these two things that cause hopelessness for beings at the time of death.
What are the two?
That is to say: one being commits or causes another to commit an evil deed;
the second, O Sarvaśūra, rejects the true Dharma.
These two beings are hopeless at the time of death.

The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said: "Venerable Blessed One, what is the destiny of those beings? What will their future state be? The Blessed One said: "Sarvaśūra, the destiny of those beings who reject the True Dharma is infinite; their future state is infinite. For an entire eon, Sarvaśūra, they shall experience painful sensations in the Raurava great hell."
For one kalpa in Saṃghāta;
for one kalpa in Tapana; for one kalpa in Pratāpana;
and for one kalpa in the Mahānaraka Kālasūtra.
For one eon in the Mahāvīci great hell; for one eon in the Romaharṣa great hell; for one eon in the Haha great hell.
(For one eon in the Tapana Great Hell): O Sarvaśūra, in these eight great hells, beings who have rejected the true Dharma must experience suffering for eight eons.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One: “Suffering, Blessed One! Suffering, Sugata! I do not venture to hear it.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
(1) Since you do not venture to hear these words of great terror—
how beings experience sensations in hell, which is exclusively suffering;
(2) whatever wholesome karma one performs, happiness shall be his lot.
Whatever unwholesome karma one performs will result only in suffering.
For one who is born, death is suffering; grief is suffering, and bondage is suffering.
Indeed, suffering is constant for the fool who does not understand the cause of happiness.
(4) Indeed, it is a happiness for the wise who remembers the supreme Buddha;
those who have clear faith in the Mahāyāna shall not go to an evil destiny.
(5) In this very way, Sarvaśūra, one is impelled by former karma.
For even a small deed performed yields infinite fruit;
just as by sowing a tiny seed one obtains abundant fruit,
so too in the Buddha-field, which is a fertile field, there is a great harvest from the seed sown.
(7) The wise find happiness and delight in the teaching of the Victor;
they avoid all evils and perform much that is wholesome.
(8) Those who shall give even as much as a hair’s breadth in charity within my teaching [shall attain this].
For eighty thousand eons, possessing great enjoyments and vast wealth,
wherever they are reborn, they always remember their giving.
Thus, indeed, this profound gift to the Buddha yields such great fruit.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should the Dharma be understood within the teaching of the Blessed One? And how, Blessed One, will a root of merit be acquired upon hearing the *Saṃghāṭa* Sūtra, this discourse on the Dharma?

The Blessed One replied: “Sarvaśūra, suppose one were to attend upon Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of twelve Ganges rivers, providing them with all the requisites for happiness.”
Whoever should hear this Dharma discourse, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, their mass of merit should be known to be exactly like that.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said: "Blessed One, how should the fulfillment of the roots of goodness be accomplished?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra: "Sarvaśūra, whatever is a root of goodness should be known as equal to the Tathāgata."
Sarvaśūra asked: “Blessed One, which root of merit is to be known as equal to the Tathāgata?

The Blessed One replied: “Sarvaśūra, the Dharma-preacher (dharmabhāṇaka) is to be known as equal to the Tathāgata. Sarvaśūra asked: “Blessed One, who is a Dharma-preacher? The Blessed One replied: “He who causes the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* to be heard is a Dharma-preacher.”
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said: "Blessed One, those who hear this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, will produce such a mass of merit;
how much more so those who write it down (or write it down themselves)?"
They will recite it.
"Blessed One, how great a mass of merit will they produce?
The Blessed One said: "Listen, Sarvaśūra!"

For example, suppose that in each of the four directions there were Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of twelve Ganges rivers, who remained for twelve kalpas as numerous as the sands of twelve Ganges rivers and taught the Dharma, describing the mass of merit of this *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* dharma-discourse; even if they were to describe it, it would be impossible to reach the limit of that mass of merit, nor could it be fully expressed by speech.

Even by Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of forty-eight Ganges rivers, it would not be possible to fully describe the mass of merit produced by one who writes this; what need is there to mention those who will read it, or those who will contemplate it, or those who will become meditators on the Dharma? The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said: "Blessed One, how great a mass of merit will those produce who read it?"
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
(10) But when a four-line verse is recited, whatever merit therein [accrues],
as many Victors (*jina*) as there are grains of sand in eighty-four Ganges rivers might remain here and describe that merit of what has been recited. (11) They might describe it, remaining steadfast.
And that merit would not be exhausted until the prophecy were received;
even if eighty million Buddhas were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges and describe all the qualities of the Mahāyāna in every direction.
And whatever merit belongs to the *Saṃghāṭa*, that shall never come to exhaustion.
Thus, the teachings of the Dharma by the Buddhas are indeed difficult to encounter and are infinite.
Furthermore, at that time and on that occasion, eighty-four hundred thousand million sons of the gods approached the Tathāgata and the exposition of the Dharma-discourse known as the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*.

Bowing with palms joined in reverence, they said this to the Blessed One: “Excellent, excellent, Blessed One! It is wonderful that the Blessed One has established such a treasury of Dharma in Jambudvīpa. Then eighteen thousand other *nirgrantha* ascetics approached the place where the Blessed One was staying. Having approached, they spoke thus to the Blessed One: “Victory to you, O Śramaṇa Gautama! The Blessed One replied: “The Tathāgata is always victorious.”
"O Nigrantha heretics, how did you, the heretics, speak of his victory?
They said, 'May the ascetic Gautama be victorious, may he indeed be victorious!'"
The Blessed One said: "I do not see victory for you. And he said:
(14) "You are established in error; how can there be victory for you? Listen, O Nirgranthas, I shall speak for your benefit."
(15) For one of childish intellect there is no happiness; what victory will there be for you?
I shall show you the profound path through the eye of a Buddha.

<50> Then those Nirgranthas, in the presence of the Blessed One, became angry and gave rise to a mind of ill-will. At that time, on that occasion, Śakra, the lord of the gods, was present and seated within that assembly; seeing those heretical Nirgranthas enraged in the presence of the Blessed One, he struck his vajra.
<51> Then those eighteen million Nirgranthas, terrified, trembling, and afflicted by great suffering and dejection, with throats choked with tears, lamented.
And the Tathāgata caused his own self to disappear from their sight.
Then those Nirgranthas, weeping with tearful faces and no longer seeing the Tathāgata, spoke this verse:
(16) There is no protector here at all, neither mother nor father likewise; we see this wilderness, with empty dwellings and no refuge. (17) There is indeed no water, nor trees, nor birds.
And we see no one here; being without a protector, we experience most terrible feelings of suffering while not beholding the Tathāgata.
Who indeed could be our refuge and protector, by whom we might be saved from this great fear?
Then, at that time and on that occasion, those eighteen koṭis of Nirgranthas rose from their seats, knelt with both knees upon the ground, and raised their voices, proclaiming this sound:
"The Tathāgata is compassionate, the Perfectly Awakened One, the supreme among bipeds;
grant us benefit and protect this wretched world!"
<53> Then the Blessed One, having manifested a smile, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra:
"Go, Sarvaśūra, and teach the Dharma to the Nigranthas and other non-Buddhist outsiders.

When this was said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One: "Is it not the case, Blessed One, that the Black Mountains bow their heads before Sumeru, the king of mountains?"
"While the Tathāgata remains present, I shall teach the Dharma.

The Blessed One said: "Enough, son of good family! The skillful means of the Tathāgatas are manifold. Go, Sarvaśūra, survey the world-systems in the ten directions; see where you perceive a Tathāgata, or where you perceive the seat of a Tathāgata prepared."
"O Sarvaśūra, I myself shall teach the Dharma to the Nirgranthas and other non-Buddhist outsiders.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said: "Venerable Blessed One, by whose miraculous power shall I go? By my own miraculous power, or by yours?"
"Or else, I shall go by means of the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
The Blessed One said, "Sarvaśūra, go by the empowerment of your own supernatural power; Sarvaśūra, come back again by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One, and vanished right there.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One taught the Dharma to those followers of other sects:
"O worthy ones, birth is suffering; birth itself is suffering. For one who has been born, many fears arise.
For one who has been born, the fear of illness arises; from illness, the fear of old age arises."
In one who is aged, the fear of death arises. They asked: "What, Blessed One, is the fear of one who is born?
The Blessed One said: "It is called 'born, born'."
For a person who is born, many fears arise: fear of kings arises, fear of thieves arises,
fear of fire arises,
and fear of poison arises.
Fear of water arises;
fear of wind arises;
fear of whirlpools arises.
"Fear arises from one's own committed actions.
While the Blessed One was thus teaching the Dharma in its many aspects concerning the origin of birth,
at that time and on that occasion, those other sectarians, the Nirgranthas, heard it.
A great terror arose, and they said: "O Blessed One, we no longer venture to experience the suffering of birth.

Now, while this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse was being spoken by the Blessed One, those eighteen *koṭis* of Nigranthas and followers of other sects became fully established in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
and within their own bodies, eighteen thousand Bodhisattvas were established in the ten great stages (*mahābhūmi*).
All of them displayed various miraculous transformations of their own bodies in many ways, namely: the form of a horse, the form of an elephant.
Some had the form of a lion, some the form of a tiger, some the form of Garuḍa, some the form of Mount Sumeru, some the form of Nandika, and some the form of a tree;
they all sat cross-legged in the lotus posture.
Nine thousand times ten million bodhisattvas sat on the right side of the Blessed One.
Nine thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas sit on the left side of the Blessed One;
yet the Tathāgata, being eternally in meditative equipoise, appears teaching the Dharma to sentient beings through skillful means.
By the seventh day and night, the Tathāgata extended his hand as if it were the palm of his own hand.
The Blessed One knew that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra was coming here from that world-system Padmottarā.
And when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra departed, he reached that world-system Padmottarā in seven days and nights through the empowerment of his own supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*).
And when the Blessed One extended his tongue far,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra stood before the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One seven times, and with a mind full of serene faith toward the Blessed One,
bowed with palms joined toward the Tathāgata and addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"I have gone, Blessed One, to all the world-systems in the ten directions. Blessed One, I have seen ninety-nine thousand million world-systems. And, Blessed One, by my first supernormal power I have seen ninety thousand million Buddha-fields, and by my second supernormal power I have seen one hundred thousand million Buddhas, the Blessed Ones."

Within seven days and nights, I arrived at that world-system Padmottarā. During this interval, I beheld thousands of millions of *akṣobhya* Buddha-fields; there, I witnessed the miraculous power of those Blessed Buddhas.
In ninety-two hundred thousand nayutas of millions of Buddha-fields, Tathāgatas were teaching the Dharma.
On that very same day, in eighty hundred thousand million Buddha-fields, eighty hundred thousand million Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas appeared in the world.
Having paid homage to all those Tathāgatas, I departed once more.
On that very same day, Blessed One, having passed beyond thirty-nine thousand million Buddha-fields, in all those thirty-nine thousand million Buddha-fields, thirty-nine...

Thousands of millions of bodhisattvas, having gone forth on that very day, fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; and those Blessed Ones, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were saluted by me, O Blessed One, and after circumambulating them three times to the right, they vanished through their supernatural power. O Blessed One, in sixty million Buddha-fields, I behold the Blessed Buddhas.
And those buddha-fields and those Blessed Buddhas were worshipped by me, O Blessed One, and from there I departed.
Furthermore, O Blessed One, in hundreds of millions of other buddha-fields I saw Tathāgatas entering final nirvāṇa;
those Tathāgatas were worshipped by me, and from there I departed.
"O Blessed One, I have seen the True Dharma disappearing in ninety-five other *koṭis* of Buddha-fields.
O Blessed One, mental anguish arose within me there, and I shed tears.
Moreover, I see many others—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and those capable of assuming any form at will—who are weeping and pierced by the great dart of sorrow."

In this way, having paid homage even to that other buddha-field—which was entirely consumed by fire, including its oceans, Mount Sumeru, and its regions of earth—I departed from there, O Blessed One, devoid of hope. Then, O Blessed One, I arrived at that world-system called Padmottarā; and in that world-system Padmottarā, O Blessed One, I saw five hundred thousand million seats prepared.
In the southern direction, I see hundreds of thousands of millions of seats prepared;
on the left side, I see hundreds of thousands of millions of seats prepared;
in the eastern direction, I see hundreds of thousands of millions of seats prepared.
In the western direction, I see one hundred thousand million seats prepared;
in the upward direction, I see one hundred thousand million seats prepared.
And, Blessed One, all those seats are made of the seven precious gems.
And upon all those seats sat Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, teaching the Dharma.
Thereupon, O Blessed One, struck with wonder, I paid homage to those Tathāgatas and asked them:
"Blessed One, what is the name of this world-system?"
Those Tathāgatas said, "Noble son, this world-system is named Padmottara.
Then, O Blessed One, having circumambulated them, I again questioned those Tathāgatas: "What is the name of the Tathāgata here in this Buddha-field?
Those Tathāgatas said, "Noble son, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Padmagarbha is the one who performs the work of a Buddha here in this Buddha-field."
Then I said to them: "Many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Tathāgatas are seen;
I do not know which one among them is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Padmagarbha.
Those Tathāgatas said: "O son of good family, we shall show that Tathāgata Padmagarbha to you."
That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Padmagarbha—
then, at that very moment, all those bodies of the Tathāgatas vanished, and all the forms of the Bodhisattvas appeared;
I saw only a single Tathāgata.
Just as I had bowed my head at the feet of that Tathāgata and stood before him, a seat appeared. And that Tathāgata said this to me:
"Sit here on this seat, son of good family."
Then, O Blessed One, as I sat upon that seat, many seats appeared;
yet I did not see anyone seated upon those seats.
Therefore, I questioned the Tathāgata.
“Blessed One, I do not see even a single being seated upon these seats.
The Blessed One said this to me:
“Noble son, beings who have not cultivated roots of merit are unable to sit upon these seats.”
I addressed that Tathāgata as follows: "Blessed One, having performed what kind of roots of merit do sentient beings sit upon these seats? He, Blessed One, spoke to me thus:
Listen, son of good family: those beings who shall hear this *Saṃghāṭa* sūtra, this discourse on the Dharma, will by virtue of that root of merit sit upon these very seats;
how much more so for those who shall write it down or recite it?
"O Sarvaśūra, because you have heard this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse, you have sat upon this seat.
Otherwise, who else in this Buddha-field would be granted entry within?
When that Blessed One had spoken thus, I said this to the Blessed One: 'Blessed One, how great a mass of merit will that being produce who [hears] this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse? "
"He shall hear it.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Padmagarbha, manifested a smile.
Regarding that, O Blessed One, I asked the Blessed One the reason for his smile: "O Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, that the Tathāgata manifests a smile?"
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, noble son Sarvaśūra, [the bodhisattva mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta].

For example, noble son, suppose there were a certain king who was a universal monarch (cakravartin), a lord of the four continents; he might sow sesame seeds throughout the fields of those four continents. What do you think, Sarvaśūra?"
"Many seeds of his would arise. Sarvaśūra said: "Many, Blessed One; many, Sugata. The Blessed One said:

Then, Sarvaśūra, suppose there were a certain being who would make those sesame seeds into a single heap, and another person who, taking a single sesame seed from that heap of sesame seeds, would place it on the second side. What do you think, Sarvaśūra? Would that being be able to count those sesame seeds or even provide a comparison for them?
Sarvaśūra, the Bodhisattva, said:
"Certainly not, Blessed One; certainly not, Sugata.
It would not be possible to count those sesame seeds," [he said].

The Blessed One said: "In the very same way, Sarvaśūra, it is impossible to make a comparison for the mass of merit belonging to this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa*, except by means of a Tathāgata."

For example, Sarvaśūra, even if there were as many Tathāgatas as there are sesame seeds, and all of them were to proclaim the merit of the roots of goodness from hearing this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa*,
the merit would not be exhausted even by way of analogy— how much more so for one who would write it down or recite it?
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said:
"Blessed One, how much merit accrues to one who writes down this Dharma-discourse?
The Blessed One replied:
Listen, son of good family!
It is as if, son of good family, there were a certain man who, in a trichiliocosm great thousandfold world system, were to cut every blade of grass or piece of wood into the size of a finger-joint.
Listen to a second simile, Sarvaśūra:

"It is just as if, for example, all the stones, precipices, earth, and even the atoms of dust within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system were each to become universal monarchs, sovereigns of the four continents, endowed with the seven treasures. What do you think, Sarvaśūra? Is it possible for all sentient beings to provide even a comparison for the mass of merit belonging to all those universal monarchs?
Sarvaśūra, the Bodhisattva, replied: "No."
"It is not possible, Blessed One, except for the Tathāgata.

The Blessed One said: "Precisely so, Sarvaśūra, it is not possible to make a comparison for the mass of merit produced by writing down this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*. The merit produced by one who writes down even a single syllable from this Dharma-discourse and preserves it is far greater than the merit of all those universal monarchs; I declare that his merit is much more vast, and not that of those kings."

In the same way, Sarvaśūra, the merit of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who upholds the true Dharma of the Mahāyāna and abides in its practice cannot be surpassed by the merits of universal monarchs (cakravartin).
Likewise, it is impossible to provide even a metaphorical comparison for the merit arising from the writing of this *Saṃghāṭa* dharma-discourse.
Sarvaśūra, this *Saṃghāṭa* Sūtra reveals stores of merit;
it pacifies all afflictions and kindles the torch of all dharmas.
He conquers all the Evil Māras;
he illumines all the abodes of the bodhisattvas; and he brings forth all the accomplishments of the dharmas.

When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "In this regard, Blessed One, the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is an extremely difficult practice. For what reason? Because, Blessed One, the practices of a Tathāgata are difficult to find; even so, the practice of celibacy is difficult to find. And when one shall practice celibacy, at that time one will behold the Tathāgata face to face."
Day and night there will be a vision of the Tathāgata.
And whenever one sees the Tathāgata, then one sees a completely pure buddha-field;
and whenever one sees a completely pure buddha-field, [one sees the Tathāgata].
Then he beholds the treasuries of all dharmas. When he beholds the treasuries of all dharmas,
then at the time of his death no fear arises in him, and he shall never again be reborn in a mother’s womb.

"He shall never experience sorrow, nor shall he be bound by the snare of craving. When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra: "What do you think, Sarvaśūra? Is it not indeed rare for Tathāgatas to appear?"
He said, "It is rare, Blessed One; it is rare, Sugata.
The Blessed One said, "In the same way, Sarvaśūra, this Dharma-discourse called Saṃghāta is rare."
Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, those to whom this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa* shall come within the range of their hearing will,
for eighty eons, be able to remember their births from lifetime to lifetime.
For sixty thousand eons, they will obtain the sovereignty of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
For eight thousand eons he will attain the status of Śakra;
for twenty-five thousand eons he will be reborn in the company of the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm;
and for thirty-eight thousand eons he will be a Mahābrahmā.
For ninety-nine thousand eons he shall not fall into the lower realms;
for a hundred thousand eons he shall not be reborn among the hungry ghosts;
and for twenty-eight thousand eons he shall not be reborn as an animal.
For thirteen thousand kalpas he will not be reborn among the hosts of asuras;
he will not die by the sword, nor by poison, nor by fire, and he shall have no fear of harm from others.
For twenty-five thousand kalpas he will not be lacking in wisdom.
For seven thousand eons he will be one who practices wisdom;
for nine thousand eons he will be pleasing to behold. His perfection of the form-body will be just like that of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
For fifteen thousand kalpas, he will not be reborn in a female body;
for sixteen thousand kalpas, illness shall not afflict his body;
and for thirty-five thousand kalpas, he will possess the divine eye.
For nineteen thousand eons he will not be reborn among the *nāga* species;
for six thousand eons he will not be overcome by anger;
and for seven thousand eons he will not be reborn in impoverished families.
For eighty thousand eons he shall enjoy two continents;
even when he becomes poor, he will still obtain such happiness.
For twelve thousand eons he shall not be reborn in the wombs of the blind.
For thirteen thousand kalpas he will not be reborn in the states of woe;
for eleven thousand kalpas he will be a proponent of patience.
At the time of death, when the final consciousness is ceasing, he will not possess perverted perceptions.
And he shall not be overcome by anger.
[84] In the eastern direction, he will see before his eyes twelve Buddhas, Blessed Ones, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā;
in the southern direction, he will see before his eyes twenty koṭis of Buddhas.
In the western direction, he will behold twenty-five times as many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, face to face.
In the northern direction, he will behold twenty times as many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, face to face.
In the zenith, he will behold ninety thousand million Buddhas, Blessed Ones, face to face.
In the direction below, he will see face-to-face a hundred koṭis of Buddhas, Blessed Ones, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
And all those Tathāgatas will comfort that son of good family, saying:
"Do not fear, son of good family; by you, the *Saṃghāṭa* [Sūtra]..."
"Having heard this Dharma discourse, there will be such benefits and advantages pertaining to the future life.
Do you see, O son of good family, these many hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of Tathāgatas, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā?
He replied, "I see them, Blessed One; I see them, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:
"O noble son, these Tathāgatas have approached you for the purpose of being seen.
He asked: "What wholesome deed have I performed, by which so many Tathāgatas have come?"

[86] He said: "Listen, noble son! Since you have obtained this human body and the *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse has come within the range of your hearing, you have thereby produced such a vast mass of merit.
Sarvaśūra said:
“If, Blessed One, even for me there is such a mass of merit, how much more so for one who shall hear it in its entirety and completion?
[87] The Blessed One said: “Enough, noble son! Listen; I shall describe the merit of hearing even a single four-line verse.”

For example, noble son, the mass of merit belonging to as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are grains of sand in thirteen Ganges rivers is surpassed by the even greater mass of merit of one who hears from this Dharma discourse even a single four-line verse;
and [it is surpassed] by one who makes offerings to as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are grains of sand in thirteen Ganges rivers.
Whoever hears from this *Cetasaṃghāṭa* discourse on Dharma even a single four-line verse shall produce a mass of merit far greater than that;
how much more so for one who hears it in its entirety and in full!
It is impossible to provide a comparison for that mass of merit.
Listen, son of good family: whoever shall hear this *Saṃghāṭa*—the discourse on the Dharma—in its entirety and in detail, [shall obtain such merit].

Suppose someone were to sow sesame seeds throughout the entire great trichiliocosm, and there were as many universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) as there were sesame grains. Now, suppose there were a certain man who was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, and that man were to give gifts to all those universal monarchs according to their every desire. What do you think, Sarvaśūra—would that man, on that account, [produce much merit]?
[The interlocutor] said: "Great merit would be produced, Blessed One; great, Sugata.

The Blessed One said: "O son of good family, compared to the mass of merit from those universal monarchs giving gifts, the merit of one who gives a gift to a single stream-enterer is much greater than that."
One generates a mass of merit.

[89] If all the beings in the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system were to become stream-enterers, and one were to give gifts to them all, the mass of merit generated by this person would be far greater than that mass of merit.
If one were to give a gift to a single once-returner,

and all the beings in a great trichiliocosm world-system were likewise to become once-returners, and one were to give a gift to all of them— the mass of merit from that is far surpassed by the mass of merit produced by this [other person].
If one were to give gifts to a single non-returner (anāgāmin),

and all the beings in a triple-thousand great thousandfold world system were to become non-returners and one were to give gifts to them all— the mass of merit from giving to all of them is far surpassed by the mass of merit produced by one who gives a gift to a single arhat (arhan).

If all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were to become arhats, and one were to give gifts to all of them, the mass of merit arising from that would be far surpassed by the mass of merit produced by one who gives a gift to a single pratyekabuddha.

If all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system were to become Pratyekabuddhas, and one were to give gifts to them all, the mass of merit resulting from that would be far surpassed by the mass of merit produced by one who gives a gift to a single Bodhisattva. Even if all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system were to become Bodhisattvas, and one were to give gifts to them all, the mass of merit resulting from that would be far surpassed by [the merit of giving to a single Bodhisattva].
One generates a mass of merit:

he who would clear his mind toward a single Tathāgata, and he who would clear his mind toward as many Tathāgatas as fill a trichiliocosm world-system, and he who shall write down this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*.
How much more so, Sarvaśūra, for one who shall hear this Dharma-discourse,
and having heard it, shall retain it, recite it, master it, and reveal it in detail to others?
How much more so, Sarvaśūra, for one who shall pay homage with a clear mind to this Dharma discourse, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*?
What do you think, Sarvaśūra, is it possible for foolish commoners to hear this sūtra?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
He said: "And those who hear it but do not produce faith?
Listen, Sarvaśūra; there are, Sarvaśūra, some beings who are foolish ordinary persons (*bālapṛthagjana*) who would be able to find the bottom of the great ocean.
He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
[92] The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, is there any being who could exhaust the ocean with a single palm of his hand?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One; certainly not, Sugata."
The Blessed One said: "Sarvaśūra, there is no sentient being whatsoever who would be able to dry up the great ocean with a single palm of the hand."

In the same way, Sarvaśūra, those beings who have inferior inclinations are not able to hear this Dharma discourse, nor, Sarvaśūra, are they able to write down this Saṃghāṭa Dharma discourse by those who have not seen hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of eighty Ganges rivers.
Those who have not seen Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of ninety Ganges rivers are unable to hear this Dharma-discourse.
Those who have not seen hundreds of thousands of millions of Tathāgatas, upon hearing this Dharma-discourse, reject it.

Sarvaśūra, those who have seen hundreds of millions of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges river, upon hearing this Dharma-discourse, give rise to a mind of serene faith and rejoice in accordance with reality.
They understand;
those who, with true faith, believe in this *Saṃghāṭa* discourse on Dharma and do not reject it.
Listen, Sarvaśūra: whatever beings write down even a single syllable or a four-line verse from this *Saṃghāṭa* discourse on Dharma, for all those beings, Sarvaśūra, after that—
Having transcended ninety-five thousand million world-systems, their buddha-field will be just like the world-system Sukhāvatī.
And, Sarvaśūra, the lifespan of all those beings will be eighty-four thousand kalpas.
Listen, Sarvaśūra: those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who shall hear from this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa* even a single four-line verse.

For example, Sarvaśūra, suppose there were a certain being who was fierce, reckless, turned away from the true Dharma, indifferent to the next world, and a doer of evil— someone who might commit, cause others to commit, or rejoice in the commission of the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karmāṇi*). If that person were to hear even a single four-line verse from this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse,
those five deeds of immediate retribution would be completely exhausted for them.
[96] Listen, Sarvaśūra!
Furthermore, I shall proclaim another quality.
For example, suppose there were some being who would cause a schism in a stūpa and a schism in the Saṅgha.

If one were to cause a bodhisattva to rise from meditative concentration, create an obstacle to the wisdom of a Buddha, or deprive his mother or father of life—and yet that being later becomes remorseful, grieving and lamenting, "I am ruined by this body; my future world is lost"—then for an entire eon he would be ruined. Consequently, he would experience great mental distress and undergo painful sensations.
He would experience bitter suffering.
O Sarvaśūra, all beings avoid and loathe that being;
he is burnt and ruined, a being lost to both mundane and supramundane Dharma for many eons, like a charred pillar.

[97] In just this way, just as a house that was once beautifully decorated does not shine when its pillars are burnt, even so this person does not shine in this world. And wherever he goes, there he is reviled by sentient beings and they strike him.
Though afflicted by hunger and thirst, he obtains nothing;
consequently, he experiences painful sensations.
On account of that hunger and thirst, as well as on account of insults and blows, he recollects his destruction of stūpas and the five actions of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*).
Thereupon, he gives rise to suffering and a mind of world-weariness:
"Where shall I go? Who will be my protector?
He thinks thus: "I shall go; I will enter the mountain caves and glens, and there my death will come to pass, for here no one is my protector."
And it is said:
(20) A wicked deed has been done by me; like a scorched pillar, it is without interval [of purity]. I shall not adorn this world, nor shall I adorn the next.
(21) I do not shine within the house, nor do I shine outside.
(22) "I am not beautiful anywhere; I am such a doer of evil. Because of the fault, I have committed sin, and by that I shall go to an evil rebirth.
Suffering in the next world, where indeed shall I dwell in that miserable state?"
The deities hear her voice as she weeps with a throat choked by tears:
"Alas! Deprived of hope, I shall depart for the next world and fall into a miserable rebirth."
The deities said to him:
(24) "You are deluded; go, O man! Do not think thus in your distress: 'I have no refuge, nor do I have a protector; I experience painful sensations.'"
(25) "I have committed the murder of my mother, the murder of my father, and the five deeds of immediate retribution; I shall go to the summit of the mountain and there I shall abandon my life.
(26) "Do not go, O foolish man! Do not perform such an evil deed!"
Much evil has been committed by you with a corrupted mind;
those who commit suicide go to hell in suffering,

Then, having sat down for that excellent moment and instant,

(34) "Eat this food which I give you; you cry out in suffering, tormented by grief."
Afflicted by hunger and thirst,

"Enjoy this delicious and pleasing food which will satisfy your body;

"I have created an obstacle to the Bodhisattva's attainment of Buddhahood.

Then, at that time, that man, pierced by the arrow of grief, frightened, terrified, and agitated, cried out, "Who will be my protector? and said:

(43) "The seer shall be my protection, and I shall be near to you. When I am free from remorse and at peace, may my evil deeds be stilled.

Listen to the Dharma in my presence. Have you ever heard the Dharma discourse named *Saṃghāṭa*?

The seer said: "Who teaches the Dharma to a being who has been consumed by fire, other than one who, dwelling in compassion, teaches the Dharma to beings?
He replied:

[101] Once upon a time, in the past,

incalculable and even more incalculable eons ago, at that time and in that age, there was a king named Vimalacandra, a righteous ruler of the Dharma. Furthermore, noble son, a son was born into the house of that King Vimalacandra.
[102] Then King Vimalacandra, having assembled the Brahmins who were experts in physiognomy, divination, and the study of the treatises, showed the prince to them and spoke thus:

Having heard this, the king asked in great agitation:

Why is that? Because at some time or other, the birth of a human being is obtained in this world."
"I shall not act in such a way that I will lose this human body. Then that prince grew; whereas others grow over two years, he grew in a single month.
And King Vimalacandra knew that the prince was growing through the accumulation of his own past actions.
Then the king, having bound the turban upon the prince, spoke thus:
"Let this kingdom be yours; exercise your vast fame, sovereignty, and royal enjoyments according to the Dharma, not according to what is unrighteous."

Then those thirty million ministers approached King Vimalacandra; having approached, they said this to King Vimalacandra: "O Great King, why do you no longer exercise sovereignty over your own realm?"

The king said: "For many incalculable eons, I exercised sovereignty, enjoyment, power, and lordship over kingdoms; yet at no time did I ever find satisfaction in sense objects. At that time, on that occasion, after no long interval, that son deprived his parents of life."
And by him, moreover, the five deeds of immediate retribution were accumulated there.
And I, O man, remember a time so long ago as if it were today or tomorrow.
When painful sensations arose for that king, he became remorseful and, with a choked throat, lamented, "I have committed a sinful deed;
I shall experience painful sensations in the great Avīci hell.
Thereupon, having conceived a mind of compassion, I went there and taught the Dharma to that king.
Then, having heard that Dharma, those five deeds of immediate retribution of that king quickly went to complete destruction without remainder.
And he said: "The *Saṃghāṭa*, a discourse on Dharma, the king of sūtras, [was taught] by the one of great asceticism."
Those who hear this Dharma will attain the unsurpassed state; all their evil deeds will be exhausted, and all their afflictions will be pacified. (45)
Listen, I shall proclaim the Dharma by which you will quickly be liberated.
(46) While this four-line verse is being recited continuously, you will bring about the destruction of all evil and become a stream-enterer.
(47) Then I uttered this gift that liberates from all evil:
"May suffering beings be released from the terrifying fear of hell.
(48) Thereupon, that man rose from his seat with palms joined in reverence.
Bowing his head to him, he offers words of praise:

[106] Then, at that time and on that occasion, twelve thousand sons of gods stationed in the sky above approached that seer with palms joined in reverence, bowed their heads at his feet, and spoke thus:

The great-souled ṛṣi said:
"I recollect hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable kalpas.
He asked: "By what wholesome karma?"
In just a single moment, this evil deed (all evil deeds) was pacified. [He said: "Upon hearing the Saṃghāṭa Dharma-discourse, by means of this wholesome deed, all evil deeds were pacified."

[108] And those beings who were assembled there, by whom this Dharma-discourse was heard and either faith was produced or conviction was attained— they are all prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
This is also true for the person by whom those five deeds of immediate retribution were committed.

Having heard this Dharma discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa*, in a mere moment, those five deeds of immediate retribution were completely exhausted, eliminated, and brought to an end. For him, the doors to the various miserable destinies remain closed for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons,
while the thirty-two doors to the celestial realms remain open.

Whoever hears even a single four-line verse from this *Saṃghāṭa* dharma-discourse shall possess such roots of merit; how much more so for one who honors, reveres, respects, and worships the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*.

Or, with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags, or by means of music, the gesture of joined palms, or prostration, they will perform an act of homage; or they will rejoice even once and speak thus:
"Excellent! Well-spoken!"

[109] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how great a mass of merit is produced by the salutation with palms joined by those who, having heard this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse being spoken, join their palms and pay homage? The Blessed One said: "Listen, son of good family! Suppose someone has committed, caused others to commit, or rejoiced in the commission of the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karmāṇi*). If that person, from this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse, should hear even a single four-line verse..."
Upon hearing this verse, he will join his palms in reverence;
all his five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) will be extinguished.
How much more so, O Sarvaśūra, for one who hears this entire Dharma-discourse in its full completion—he shall produce a mass of merit far greater than that.
[110] O son of good family, I shall provide a simile for you so that you may understand the meaning of this *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*.
It is just as, for example, in the abode of the nāga king Anavatapta, the sun never shines.
And from there, five great rivers flow.

Now, suppose there were a certain person who were to count the drops of water from those five great rivers. What do you think, Sarvaśūra, would it be possible for you to calculate those drops of water?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One; certainly not, Sugata."

The Blessed One said: "In this very way, Sarvaśūra, it is not possible to reach the limit of the root of merit of this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, by means of calculation—even in an eon, or a hundred eons, or a thousand eons, or a hundred thousand eons, or even a hundred thousand times ten million billion eons.
What do you think, Sarvaśūra, is it difficult for one who would proclaim this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa*, for even a moment?"
He said, "It is difficult, Blessed One; it is difficult, Sugata.

The Blessed One said, "Sarvaśūra, it is even more difficult than that for one who will be able to hear this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa*, just as [it is difficult to draw water] from the great lake Anavatapta."
Five great rivers flow;

it is not possible for anyone, whether a mathematician or a chief mathematician, to reach the limit of the drops of water from those five great flowing rivers through calculation. In the very same way, it is not possible to reach the limit of the mass of merit of this Dharma discourse.
Sarvaśūra said: "Blessed One, what are those five great rivers? The Blessed One replied: "They are as follows:
the Gaṅgā, the Sītā, the Vakṣu, the Yamunā, and the Candrabhāgā."
Sarvaśūra, these five great rivers enter the great ocean;
and each individual great river has a retinue of five hundred great rivers.
[113] Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, these five great rivers flow through the sky;
they constantly and continuously flood the world with drops of water.
And each of those five great rivers has a retinue of one thousand.
He asked: "Blessed One, what are those five great rivers with their thousandfold retinues that flow through the sky?
The Blessed One replied: "The river named Sundarī has a thousandfold retinue."
The river named Śaṅkhā has a retinue of a thousand [rivers],
as does the river named Vahantī.
The river named Citrasenā with its thousandfold retinue,
and [the river] with its thousandfold retinue.
The river named Dharmavṛttā has a retinue of one thousand;
these, O Sarvaśūra, are the five great rivers with their retinues of one thousand each that bring about activity in Jambūdvīpa.
Those rain-showers which, from time to time, release drops over Jambūdvīpa,
by means of them the flowers, fruits, and crops flourish; when [the drops] fall upon Jambūdvīpa...
Showers fall;
then water is produced. Once produced, that water satisfies all fields and groves and brings them happiness.
Sarvaśūra, it is just as, for example, a sovereign lord (*prajāpati*) brings happiness to all of Jambūdvīpa;
even so, Sarvaśūra, this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa* has been proclaimed in Jambūdvīpa for the benefit of many people and for the happiness of many people.
And just as the measure of the lifespan of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven is not the same as that of humans, so it is with this.
In that regard, Sarvaśūra, who are the Trāyastriṃśa gods where Śakra, the lord of the gods, dwells?
Those known as the Trāyastriṃśa gods are, for example, Sarvaśūra, those beings who utter even a single virtuous word.
It is impossible to make a comparison for their mass of merit (which results in the incomparable happiness they experience among gods and humans).

[115] Sarvaśūra, there are beings who utter even a single word of verbal misconduct; it is impossible to make a comparison for the suffering those beings undergo in the hells, the animal realm, and as hungry ghosts.
They experience sensations, yet there is no protector for them; falling into the hells, they lament there in despair. This should be understood as being due to the influence of unwholesome friends.
As for those beings who speak well-conducted speech, it is impossible to make a comparison for their mass of merit.
That should be understood as being due to the power of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). When one sees the spiritual friend, then the Tathāgata is seen;
when one sees the Tathāgata, [the spiritual friend is seen].
Then his all evil is destroyed.
When all evil is destroyed,
then Prajāpati exerts himself for Jambūdvīpa.

it is impossible to provide an analogy for the happiness of the beings in Jambudvīpa; in just this way, Sarvaśūra, this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa* performs the work of a Buddha for the beings of Jambudvīpa.
At that time, it would not be possible to provide a comparison for the mass of merit of those beings.
Sarvaśūra, it is just as if there were these five great rivers where they meet and converge;
in that case, it would be impossible to grasp the measure of the water.

Whether it be this many water jars, or hundreds of water jars, or thousands of water jars, or hundreds of thousands of water jars— nevertheless, because of the abundance of water, it is reckoned as a "great mass of water. Having heard it, they will take it up, retain it, recite it, master it,
and they will also reveal it in detail to others and fulfill it through practice.

At that time, it would not be possible to grasp the measure of the mass of merit of those beings; rather, because of the abundance of their merit, it is reckoned as a "great mass of merit. Sarvaśūra, those beings who do not hear this *Saṃghāṭa* discourse on Dharma will not be able to realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; they will not be able to turn the wheel of Dharma; they will not be able to strike the gong of Dharma; and they will not be able to ascend the lion-throne of Dharma.

To enter the realm of *nirvāṇa*, it is impossible for those who do not hear this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse to illuminate it with immeasurable rays of light; they are unable to sit at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Sarvaśūra said: “I ask, Blessed One; I ask, Sugata.”
Out of some curiosity, the Blessed One said: "Ask whatever you desire, Sarvaśūra; I shall remove all your doubts.

The Blessed One said:

(51) Out of compassion, the *Saṃghāṭa* manifests the form of a Buddha,

by him the *Saṃghāṭa* should be heard;
for the *Saṃghāṭa* is equal to the Buddha.
"Buddhas will always be present wherever the *Saṃghāṭa* resides.
The Blessed One said: "Listen, son of good family!
In the past, Sarvaśūra, I recall ninety-nine incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) ago."
(Therein) there were twelve crores of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Ratnottama. At that time, at that moment, I was Pradānaśūra, known by the name Candra.

according to what was appropriate for the Tathāgatas, I worshipped them with perfumes, garlands, ointments, ornaments, and decorations. And there I received the prophecy of my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. [123] Sarvaśūra, I remember thirty koṭis of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Śikhisaṃbhava, who appeared in the world.

I honored those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, with worship and respect as was their due, and it was right there that I received the prediction of my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; yet even then, the time and occasion for that prediction had not yet arrived.

[124] Sarvaśūra, I recall that twenty koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Kāśyapa appeared in the world. There, I too was Pradānaśūra, and I performed service for those Tathāgatas. I attended them with incense, garlands, and ointments, serving them with the reverence due to a Tathāgata; I acted exactly as one should act toward the Tathāgatas with profound respect.
And it was right there that I received the prediction of my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Sarvaśūra, I recall that sixteen koṭis of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Vimalaprabhāsa appeared. At that time, at that period, I was a householder—wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, one who renounced all his possessions (a great renouncer).
And those sixteen billion Buddhas were honored by me with bedding, coverings, perfumes, garlands, ointments, ornaments, and garments.
Just as service to the Tathāgatas ought to be performed, so was it performed by me.
And right there, I received the prophecy of my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
And neither was it the right time nor the proper occasion for me to give the prophecy.
[126] Listen, Sarvaśūra! I recall that ninety-five koṭis of Buddhas appeared in the world, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Śākyamuni.
And at that time, at that very moment, I was a king, a righteous Dharma-king; I attended upon them.
There were ninety-five koṭis of Tathāgatas named Śākyamuni whom I honored with incense, garlands, ointments, coverings, excellent cloths, and with parasols, banners, and flags;
and it was right there that I received the prediction of my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
[127] Sarvaśūra, I recall that ninety koṭis of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Krakutsunda appeared in the world.
At that time and on that occasion, I was a young Brahmin, wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, a giver of gifts who renounced all his own possessions.
And I attended upon all those Tathāgatas with incense, garlands, ointments, rugs, coverings, ornaments, and clothing.

And whatever kind of service was rendered to the Tathāgatas (in that same way, I performed service for them as was appropriate), right there I received the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet there was neither a lapse of time nor an inappropriate occasion for that prophecy.
[128] Sarvaśūra, I remember eighteen koṭis of Buddhas who appeared in the world;

all were Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Kanakamuni. And at that time, on that occasion, I was Pradānaśūra. I attended upon those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and I honored them with incense, garlands, ointments, rugs, coverings, and ornaments.

Just as they attended upon the Tathāgatas, so did I attend upon them; and right there I received the prophecy of my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, yet neither the time nor the occasion for that prophecy had arrived. Sarvaśūra, I recall that thirteen koṭis of Buddhas appeared in the world.
All those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were named Vabhāsaśiri. I made offerings to those Tathāgatas with rugs, robes, incense, garlands, ointments, coverings, and ornaments;

I served them in such a way that I performed the service due to a Teacher for the Tathāgatas. Those Tathāgatas also taught various gateways to the Dharma, including the definitive determination of the meaning and the Vinaya.
Right there, I received the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, yet even now the time for that prediction has not arrived.
[130] Sarvaśūra, I recall that twenty-five koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Puṣya appeared in the world;
and at that time, at that moment, I had gone forth as a renunciant and attended upon those Tathāgatas just as Ānanda now attends to my service.

Such were those Tathāgatas who attended upon me, and it was right there that I received the prophecy of my unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; yet even now, the time for my own prophecy had not yet arrived. Sarvaśūra, I recall eighteen koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas named Vipaśyin who appeared in the world;
I served those Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas with ornaments, clothing, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments, just as one should attend upon a Tathāgata.

And at that time, on that occasion, I had gone forth as a renunciant; it was there that I received the prophecy of my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, yet even now the time for that prophecy has not arrived—it will be before long.
The last Vipaśyin who appeared in the world spoke this Saṃghāṭa Dharma-discourse; having understood it, at that time I caused a rain of the seven precious gems to fall upon Jambudvīpa.

When he had rained [the jewels], those beings of Jambudvīpa became free from poverty; and right there I received the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Yet, after that long period of time, even until now, he has not predicted me [with the prediction of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena].

[133] He asked: “Blessed One, what was that time? What was that occasion? The Blessed One said: “Listen, Sarvaśūra! Two incalculable eons ago, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Dīpaṃkara appeared in the world. At that time and on that occasion, Sarvaśūra, I was a young brahmin student named Megha. And when the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, had appeared in the world, at that time I too—”
At that time, on that occasion, I practiced the holy life in the form of a young brahmin.

Then, having seen the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, I attained serene faith and scattered seven blue lotuses over him; and that root of merit planted under the Tathāgata was dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And that Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara prophesied: "O young brahmin, in a future time, after incalculable eons, you shall become a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha.

Then, O Sarvaśūra, standing twelve *tāla* trees high in the sky, I attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). And as for what I [attained], O Sarvaśūra, throughout incalculable eons—
I have practiced the holy life (brahmacarya).
Whatever roots of merit (kuśalamūla) are connected with the perfections (pāramitā), I remember them all as if they were present before me today or tomorrow.
Therein, Sarvaśūra, I established many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings in wholesome states (kuśaladharma).

What need is there to mention, Sarvaśūra, that I—who have now attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, who desire the welfare of all beings, and who am compassionate—should teach the dharma of cessation to sentient beings? Such a thing is impossible.
Why is that? Sarvaśūra, it is because I teach the dharma to sentient beings in many different ways.
I teach the Dharma in whatever form is appropriate for those beings who are to be disciplined.
In the world of the gods, I teach the Dharma to the gods in the form of a god.
In the abode of the nāgas, in the form of a nāga, I teach the Dharma to the nāgas; in the abode of the yakṣas, in the form of a yakṣa, [I teach the Dharma to the yakṣas].
I teach the Dharma;
in the realm of hungry ghosts, in the form of a hungry ghost, I teach the Dharma to the hungry ghosts.
In the world of humans, I teach the Dharma in human form to humans;
to those beings who are to be disciplined by a Buddha, I teach the Dharma in the form of a Buddha.
To those beings who are to be disciplined by a bodhisattva, I teach the Dharma in the form of a bodhisattva;
to those beings who are to be disciplined by a śrāvaka, I teach the Dharma in the form of a śrāvaka.
In whatever form beings may be led to discipline, in that very form I teach the Dharma to those beings.

In this way, Sarvaśūra, I teach the Dharma to sentient beings in many different ways. Why is that? Because, Sarvaśūra, just as sentient beings hear the Dharma in many different ways, so too do those who are the essence of sentient beings teach the Dharma to sentient beings in many different ways.
And those beings plant roots of merit in those Tathāgatas;
they give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.
They will be vigilant regarding their own welfare,
they will cultivate the recollection of death,
and they will perform such wholesome karmic formations.

And by that very cause—the roots of merit from hearing the Dharma—they will remember those previous roots of merit. That will be for their long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness, as well as for that of gods and humans.
For it is thus, Sarvaśūra, that merely upon hearing this Dharma discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, there arise such immeasurable and incalculable [qualities].
There will be these benefits and praises.
