Then those beings said to one another: "Is there some other wholesome fruit of dharma, by the performance and accumulation of which one awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and becomes a seeker of the welfare of all beings?"

[138] Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those beings, said this to them: "Noble sons, there are those who have faith in the Dharma; they will speak thus: 'The Dharma exists as it truly is. For them, there will be great fruit, a ripening of happiness, and the unsurpassed bliss of the Dharma.
[139] Those beings who are deluded by ignorance will speak thus:
"There are no phenomena, nor is there anyone who has gone beyond phenomena. For them, this will result in a great fruit with bitter ripening, and they will be reborn in the states of woe;
furthermore, those deluded persons will repeatedly be destined for the realms of misery.
For eight eons they will experience the painful sensations of hell-beings;
for twelve eons they will experience painful sensations in the wombs of hungry ghosts;
and for sixteen eons they will be reborn among the asuras.
For nine thousand kalpas they will be reborn among the classes of bhūtas and piśācas;
for fourteen thousand kalpas they will be tongueless;
and for sixteen thousand kalpas they will die within their mother’s womb.
For twelve thousand kalpas they will exist as mere lumps of flesh;
for eleven thousand kalpas they will be born blind,
experiencing painful sensations.
[141] And seeing him born blind, his parents will think:

"In vain have we experienced suffering; in vain has a son been born to us; in vain for nine months were we carried him in our womb, enduring cold and heat, and experiencing the pains of hunger and thirst."
And having experienced many sufferings to be felt in this very life, and seeing that a son has not been born, the parents will not be made anxious for the household nor for their own bodies;
consequently, great despair will arise for the parents.

In the same way, Sarvaśūra, those beings who reject the true Dharma will be hopeless and destined for the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; at the time of their death, they will be pierced by the great dart of sorrow. Sarvaśūra, those beings who speak such words as "the Dharma exists" and "there is one who has gone to the further shore of the Dharmas," by that root of merit, will be reborn in Uttarakuru for twenty eons.
For twenty-five thousand kalpas, they will be reborn in the company of the Trāyastriṃśa gods. After passing away from among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, they will be reborn in Uttarakuru;
moreover, they will not be reborn within a mother’s womb.
And they shall behold hundreds of thousands of world-systems;
having seen all those world-systems named Sukhāvatī, which display all Buddha-fields, and having established themselves right there, they shall attain awakening right there.

[143] For thus, Sarvaśūra, is the great power of this Dharma-discourse called Saṃghāṭa; those who shall produce a serene confidence of mind toward it will never pass away through an untimely or violent death. Those beings will be endowed with perfectly pure ethical discipline.
[144] They will exist, Sarvaśūra. There are beings who will say: "Day and night the Tathāgata liberates many beings;
even now, the realm of beings does not reach exhaustion."
Many make the vow for enlightenment;
many are reborn in the heavenly world;
many attain final liberation.
Now, by what cause does the exhaustion of sentient beings not occur?

II. Maitreyaparipṛcchā. [145] Then this thought occurred to the other non-Buddhist wanderers, mendicants, and Nirgranthas: "We shall go and engage in debate with the ascetic Gautama. Thereupon, ninety-four thousand Brahmins and other non-Buddhist wanderers, mendicants, and many hundreds of Nirgranthas set out for the great city of Rājagṛha.
And at that time, on that occasion, the Blessed One manifested a smile.

[146] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, for manifesting this smile?
For Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not manifest a smile without a cause or a condition."
The Blessed One said: "Listen, son of good family! Today, in this great city of Rājagṛha, a great assembly will take place.
He asked: "Who, Blessed One, will come here? Will they be gods, or nāgas, or yakṣas, or humans, or non-humans?"
The Blessed One said: "Maitreya and all these others will come here today.

Eighty-four thousand brahmins, as well as gods, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and non-humans, will come here. Nine billion heterodox practitioners—carakas, parivrājakas, and nirgranthas—will also come here."
They will engage in disputes with me;
for the sake of pacifying the disputes of them all, I shall teach the Dharma,
and all those brahmins will generate the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Ninety trillion followers of other sects—wandering mendicants, brahmins, and Nirgranthas—all shall attain the fruit of stream-entry.
Eighteen thousand million dragon kings will come;
they shall hear the Dharma from me.
And having heard it,
they will all resolve their minds toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Sixty thousand million sons of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa realm will come.
The Wicked Māra will come with his retinue consisting of thirty-two thousand koṭis;
twelve thousand koṭis of asura kings will also arrive, along with about five [thousand].
Hundreds of kings, together with their retinues, will come to hear the Dharma;
having heard the Dharma from me, they will all resolve their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
[151] Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and circumambulated the Blessed One three times, vanished right there.

III. Sarvaśūraparipṛcchā (2) [152] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what are the names of these five hundred kings?"
The Blessed One said: "Listen, Sarvaśūra! There was a king named Nanda, a king named Sunanda, a king named Upananda, and a king named Jinarṣabha."
The king named Brahmasena;
the king named Brahmaghoṣa;
the king named Sudarśana.
A king named Jayasena; a king named Nandasena;
a king named Bimbisāra.
There was a king named Prasenajit,
a king named Virūḍhaka,
and five hundred kings headed by these two.

Each king had a retinue of twenty thousand *koṭīs*, and they had all set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—with the exception of King Virūḍhaka. From the eastern direction, thirty thousand *koṭīs* of bodhisattvas arrived;
from the southern direction, fifty thousand *koṭīs* of bodhisattvas arrived.
From the western direction, sixty thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas arrive;
from the northern direction, eighty thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas arrive;
and from the downward direction, ninety thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas arrive.
From the upward direction, hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas arrived;
all of them were established on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Then all those bodhisattvas approached the great city of Rājagṛha, the Vulture Peak Mountain (*Gṛdhrakūṭaparvata*), and where the Blessed One was, in order to see and pay homage to the Blessed One.
And all those bodhisattvas had set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sarvaśūra:
"Go, Sarvaśūra, and speak thus to the bodhisattvas in all the world-systems throughout the ten directions."

"Today the Tathāgata is teaching the Dharma in the great city of Rājagṛha. Therefore, all of you who dwell in the world-systems of the ten directions, join your palms in reverence; and having heard this, return in just a moment to listen to the Dharma."

[157] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and vanished through the power of his supernatural faculties.
[158] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra, having gone to the world-systems in the ten directions, addressed the Bodhisattvas there.

"Today, friends, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, is teaching the Dharma to sentient beings in the great city of Rājagṛha within the Sahā world-system. Therefore, you should offer your approval; for this very day, it will be for your benefit, your happiness, and a great gain."
[159] Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra, having gone to the world-systems in the ten directions and attended upon all the Buddhas, announced it to the Bodhisattvas:
"Just as a strong man might snap his fingers, in that very instant the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra came to the great city of Rājagṛha, where the Blessed One was."

Standing before the Blessed One, all the brahmins, heterodox teachers, carakas, parivrājakas, and nirgranthas had assembled there; many gods, nāgas, humans, and non-humans were also gathered, as were about five hundred kings with their retinues,
and thirty-three thousand billions of Māras, the Evil Ones, together with their retinues.
[160] Then, at that time, the great city of Rājagṛha trembled. Furthermore, divine sandalwood powder rained down in the world-systems of the ten directions, and a rain of divine flowers fell.
That [powder] formed a gabled pavilion above the crown of the Blessed One’s head. At that very moment, Śakra, the lord of the gods, struck his vajra in the presence of the Tathāgata.

[161] Then, at that time, four great winds from the four directions arose in agitation. They blew away all the refuse, dust, and sand within the great city of Rājagṛha, casting it all outside the city.
Furthermore, they caused a rain of fragrant water to fall throughout the world-systems in the ten directions.
In the world-systems of the ten directions, rains of utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka lotuses fell;
those flowers remained as flower-parasols above the heads of those beings.
And above the head of the Tathāgata, in the sky overhead, eighty-four thousand gabled pavilions were established.
And within those eighty-four thousand flower-pavilions, eighty-four thousand seats made of the seven precious gems appeared, having been prepared.
Upon every seat sat a Tathāgata, teaching the Dharma. Then, indeed, this trichiliocosm great world-system shook in six ways.

[162] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra, having bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, for such miraculous displays as these being seen in the great city of Rājagṛha?"

The Blessed One said: "Suppose, for example, there were a certain man who was fickle and frivolous, established in the notions of 'I' and 'mine,' and he were poor. Now, the king might stroke his head; then that man, out of excessive pride, having gone to the royal gate, would wish to enter the royal palace by force. Then the king’s ministers and courtiers would seize that man and beat him in many ways."

[163] Then, at that time and on that occasion, if that king were to hear this report—that the poor man desires to enter the interior by force—he would think upon hearing it: "This man certainly intends to have me killed.
Thereupon, the king, being incensed, would say to his attendants: "Go, sirs, take this man to a mountain cave and deprive him of life."
Bring about the ruin of his entire retinue, including his parents, sons, daughters, female and male slaves,
and laborers. Then, they would all be deprived of life,
and all his circle of kinsmen and relatives would be pierced by the dart of supreme sorrow.
[164] In the very same way, Sarvaśūra, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, teaches the Dharma to sentient beings.
In this regard, just as that man was conceited, so too do foolish common people perceive the body of the Tathāgata by grasping at signs—such as his physical form, color, marks, and shape.
[165] There, having heard many teachings, they fall into conceit and utter various kinds of idle chatter.
Overcome by the notions of "I" and "mine," sentient beings do not themselves listen to or proclaim the Dharma.
Should anyone announce to them even a single sutra, a verse, or at least a parable, [they would reject it].
They do not grasp it and do not lend an ear, thinking, "We know this for ourselves.
For what reason? It is because they are full of conceit, and due to their great learning, they fall into negligence.
Those who associate with foolish commoners will not hear such speech endowed with the Dharma;
because of that great learning, they will become negligent.
Those such persons establish their own poems;
they establish their own books as gifts.
They bring about discord between the entire world and themselves.
They will consume a vast amount of the nation's provisions in vain;
having consumed them, they will not properly digest them,
and at the time of their death, they will experience great terror.
And those beings will say to him:
"Many of us have been taught by you the knowledge of crafts; how is it that you are not able to support yourself?
He would say this to them: "Friends, it is not possible for me to support myself at this time."
[168] There, having heard what he has spoken, those beings will lament in various ways:
"For the sake of that one individual, many innocent assemblies of kinsmen have been deprived of life through the condition of their own karma."

In the same way, at the time of death, those beings, while lamenting and perceiving themselves as destined for the realms of hell or the animal womb because of their association with evil friends, [suffer]. O brahmins—whether you be followers of other sects, wanderers, mendicants, or naked ascetics—I say this to you: do not be heedless! It is just as a bird whose wings have not yet grown is unable to traverse the sky or proceed toward the world of the gods.
In the very same way, as long as you remain established in the notions of "I" and "mine," it is not possible for you to attain nirvāṇa, nor does such supernatural power exist for you.
Why is that? Because, due to the nature of your karma, you have been born like those of the chicken womb; before long, this body will be subject to disintegration and will culminate in death.
At the time of death, there will be a lack of relish and great distress:
"Why have we maintained this physical existence, we who shall neither experience the happiness of the gods nor the happiness of the human world,
nor shall we abide in the state of nirvāṇa?"
We have carried this body in vain;
what will be our destiny, who will be our refuge, where will be our rebirth, and where [our end]?
There will be cessation.
Then the Blessed One addressed those other sectarians, wandering mendicants, naked ascetics, and brahmins once again.
"Friends, do not become hopeless regarding this Jambudvīpa made of jewels;
do not be excluded from this jewel of the Dharma.
Ask the Tathāgata whatever you desire, friends, and I shall fulfill all your intentions."
[171] Then indeed, all those brahmins, other sectarians, wanderers, mendicants, and naked ascetics rose from their seats, draped their robes over one shoulder, joined their palms in reverence,
and questioned the Blessed One: "Blessed One, day and night the Tathāgata liberates many beings from saṃsāra."
Nor is there any decrease or increase in the realm of sentient beings perceived.
Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, that these sentient beings, being equal [in nature], manifest arising and cessation?
(The *Sarvaśūraparipṛcchā* within the *Saṃghāṭa* Great Dharma-discourse is completed.
IV. The *Bhaiṣajyasenaparipṛcchā*.
[172] Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena.
The non-Buddhists don the great armor for the sake of dispelling great remorse and for the purpose of kindling the great torch of the Dharma.

They inquire about the cause of the great questions: "Listen, sons of good family! Here, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element are infinite and boundless; yet the realm of sentient beings is even more infinite than these. There are sentient beings who, for the sake of the welfare of beings, will appear in the final age to manifest arising and cessation—beings whether young or old who will bring about arising and cessation."
Bhaiṣajyasena, there are beings who, though old, are like children and know nothing at all.
Bhaiṣajyasena, it is just as if some man were to wash his head, put on new clothes, and go out from his house; then beings would address him.
"Your new garments are well-covered.
Now, suppose there were another being who would wash his head and, having washed his old garments, put them on;
yet those [old garments] would become loose and would not look beautiful.
And that man has his head well-washed, yet his garment does not shine.
In the very same way, Bhaiṣajyasena, there are aged beings who do not adorn Jambūdvīpa;
rather, it is the young beings who manifest arising and passing away.
[174] Then all those followers of other paths—the Carakas, Parivrājakas, Nirgranthas, and Brāhmaṇas—rose from their seats and said this to the Blessed One: “Who among us, Blessed One, is old?

The Blessed One said: “You are the old ones, for even now you have not attained satisfaction after repeatedly witnessing the painful sensations experienced in the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.”

[175] Then indeed, all those brahmins, heterodox practitioners, wandering mendicants, naked ascetics, and all the dragon kings said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, we no longer have the strength to experience the painful sensations within saṃsāra.
And those heterodox practitioners, wandering mendicants, naked ascetics, and brahmins spoke thus: "There are no young beings who are capable of realizing the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā)."
[176] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One: "Behold, Venerable Blessed One, how difficult it is for these beings to have faith!
The Blessed One said: "Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena; now the Tathāgata shall make it manifest before the whole world.
[177] Then ninety-four thousand koṭis of new beings stood before the Tathāgata, yet they did not salute the Tathāgata, nor did they speak to him, nor converse with him.

They consented by remaining silent. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, that these beings do not address the Blessed One, do not converse with him, do not pay him homage, and do not question the Blessed One?"
The Blessed One said: "Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena! Those beings who say, 'It is not possible for new beings to directly realize the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā),' [speak thus]."
"Bhaiṣajyasena, these beings who are new should be seen by you.
And those beings said: 'Venerable Blessed One, we are new beings; Venerable Sugata, we are new beings.
The Blessed One said: 'O beings, now demonstrate to the world, before its very eyes, the measure of your own bodies.'"

[178] Furthermore, at that time and on that occasion, ninety-four thousand koṭis of newly ordained beings, upon the dissolution of their bodies, remained in the intermediate space having attained the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One: "Well-gained are the gains, O Blessed One, for those beings who exert vigor for the exhaustion and the complete termination of saṃsāra."
O Blessed One, it is this very day that these beings have been born; O Blessed One, it is this very day that these beings have been fully liberated;
[it is this very day] that all are seen established upon the ten stages.

[179] Then indeed, all the brahmins, followers of other sects, wandering mendicants, and Nirgranthas, as well as the dragon kings and Māra the Evil One together with his retinue, approached in order to deprive [the Buddha] of his sight.

And they all said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, we have come here into the presence of the Tathāgata in order to deprive him of his sight. But having heard this Dharma discourse, Blessed One, we have attained serene confidence in both the Buddha and the Dharma."
In that regard, O Blessed One, may all of us likewise obtain such a Buddha-happiness as this from the Blessed One.
"May we likewise become Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas in the world.

The Blessed One said, "It is so, gentle sirs; it is just as you have come into the presence of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha. Having heard this Dharma discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa*, you have generated the resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
"By this root of merit, O gentle-faced ones, you shall before long fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. As soon as these words were spoken by the Blessed One,

at that very moment, all those heterodox practitioners, wandering mendicants, ascetics, and brahmins attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and they all became established on the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).

All those bodhisattvas became transformed, and they all rose into the air to the height of seven palm trees; there, they presented gabled palaces made of the seven precious gems to the Tathāgata, and they all performed various miraculous manifestations, empowerments, and supernormal feats.
Then, at that very moment, they all stood above the crown of the Blessed One’s head and scattered various flowers over him.

They bring the Tathāgatas to mind and conceive the perception of the Buddha within their own bodies; and many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sons of gods scatter divine flowers over the Tathāgata.
And they spoke these words:

"Great is the gain for the śramaṇa Gautama! A great field is the Lord of the World, who has attained the empowerment of the power of meditative concentration; he is wise and seeks the welfare of the wise, for by means of such skillful means, he gradually liberates beings from saṃsāra—even with a single well-spoken word, so many beings are liberated from saṃsāra."
[183] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground,

and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, that these sons of the gods utter such words and perform so many miraculous feats?"
And with many hymns praising his qualities, they extolled the Tathāgata. The Blessed One said: "Listen, son of good family; it is not that they are praising me.
They are praising their own bodies."
They will establish their very own bodies upon the throne of the Dharma King; they will establish their very own bodies upon the seat of the supreme Dharma;
and from their very own bodies, they will emit the rays of the Dharma.
They will be taken into the care of all the Buddhas for the sake of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and having awakened, they will teach the Dharma.

[184] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, there are many beings; Venerable Sugata, there are many beings who are liberated day and night, yet even now there is no exhaustion of beings.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Bhaiṣajyasena, that you consider it necessary to ask the Tathāgata about this matter."

Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena! It is just as if, Bhaiṣajyasena, there were a certain man who was wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments, with abundant wealth; one endowed with much money, grain, treasuries, and storehouses; one who had many male and female slaves, laborers, and servants; and who possessed many heaps of wealth, many fields and groves, and much money and grain—namely, barley, wheat, rice, sesame, beans, mung beans, and so forth—and that man, during the spring season, would sow all those grains and riches.
Then, after some time, when all that wealth and grain had ripened, he, knowing them to be ripe, would have them brought into the inner house;
that man would store those riches and grains separately within the house, and having stored them, he would enjoy them.
Just as one sows those seeds once again during the spring season,

even so, Bhaiṣajyasena, these beings, having previously performed virtuous deeds, later seek a field of merit and plant roots of goodness again and again, once the power of those former deeds has been exhausted.
Having planted roots of virtue and having practiced those wholesome dharmas therein, they bring them to fulfillment. Being perfected in practice, they cause all dharmas to increase.
Having caused all dharmas to increase, they give rise to joy and gladness.
And by that mind of joy and gladness, Bhaiṣajyasena, many thousands of millions of eons are not wasted.
In the same way, Bhaiṣajyasena, a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening never possesses a nature subject to destruction;
in brief, he understands all dharmas.
[186] He asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening see a dream?
The Blessed One said:
"Bhaiṣajyasena, a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening sees many terrors within his dreams."
For what reason? When one sees fears within a dream, at that time one purifies all sinful karmas.
Bhaiṣajyasena, it is not possible for a sentient being with sinful karma to remove intense suffering; yet, because of the sinful dream seen, no fear arises for him.
[187] Bhaiṣajyasena said: "Lord, what kinds of terrors does a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening see in his dreams?
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, he sees a blazing fire.
Thereupon, that bodhisattva should produce this thought: 'All my afflictions have been burnt away. Second, Bhaiṣajyasena, he sees water that is turbid and thoroughly agitated."
In that regard, that bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening must not be discouraged.
Why is that? Because, Bhaiṣajyasena, when a bodhisattva has thus turned back all the bonds of delusion, all evil is brought to exhaustion.
Thirdly, Bhaiṣajyasena, a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening sees a dream of great terror.
He asked: "Which one, Blessed One? The Blessed One said: "He sees his own head shaved on his body.

In that regard, Bhaiṣajyasena, that bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening must not be discouraged. Why is that? He should produce this thought: 'Lust, hatred, and delusion are mine.'"
The [roots of unwholesomeness] will be shorn away;
the saṃsāra of the six realms of existence will be conquered by me,
and indeed, there will be no dwelling in hell for him.

Bhaiṣajyasena, a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening does not take rebirth among animals, nor among hungry ghosts, nor among asuras, nor among nāgas, nor even among the pure buddhafields of the gods.
[189] Bhaiṣajyasena, in the future time, in the final age, if any sentient being should direct their mind toward awakening,
they should regard that as a great reproach.
And there will be a life of being despised.
In that regard, Bhaiṣajyasena, the bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening should not give rise to a mind of weariness, nor should he be discouraged.
[190] Bhaiṣajyasena, many dharmas have been taught by me; and Bhaiṣajyasena, for many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, I have practiced difficult austerities. But by me, Bhaiṣajyasena—

"Bhaiṣajyasena, I have practiced austerities for the sake of royal enjoyment, or for the sake of livelihood and enjoyment, or for the sake of the enjoyment of sovereignty; I have practiced austerities for the sake of awakening to the nature of phenomena. Yet, Bhaiṣajyasena, I did not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment as long as I had not heard this Dharma-discourse. But at the time, Bhaiṣajyasena, when I heard this *Saṃghāṭa*..."
On that very day, Bhaiṣajyasena, this profound Dharma discourse was heard by me, and I fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. This Dharma discourse, Bhaiṣajyasena, is profound;

its hearing is difficult to obtain even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons. Bhaiṣajyasena, the appearance of Tathāgatas is extremely rare, and Bhaiṣajyasena, one who upholds this Dharma discourse is extremely rare.
[191] Those who shall hear this Dharma-discourse,
all of them will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Bhaiṣajyasena, for a hundred thousand eons, those beings will turn their backs upon saṃsāra.
They shall obtain a completely pure buddha-field,
they shall realize the path to cessation,
and they will be capable of understanding the basis [of that realization].
They are capable of discerning the basis of the wholesome;
they are capable of discerning the basis of the wholesome pertaining to the higher knowledges; they are capable of discerning the cessation of the basis of the wholesome.
"Bhaiṣajyasena, for what purpose is 'cessation' itself so called?"
He said: "Blessed One, what is called the 'abode of the Dharma'?
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, what is the abode of the Dharma?
He said: "Blessed One, 'Dharma' refers to the exertion of vigor."
The undertaking of ethical discipline and the possession of ethical discipline is called the "treasury of Dharma. Blessed One, this treasury of Dharma comes into being.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Bhaiṣajyasena, that you consider it necessary to ask the Tathāgata about this matter.
He asked: "For what reason, Blessed One, do the Tathāgatas arise in the world?"
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, those who understand the possession of great learning understand the arising of the Tathāgatas.
Having understood the arising of the Tathāgatas, they understand this state of happiness that constitutes the arising of the Tathāgatas."
And when Tathāgatas arise in the world, then sentient beings come to understand all phenomena;
they understand the phenomena that consist of skill in means;
they understand mundane and supramundane phenomena.
They understand mundane and supramundane knowledges.
He asked: "Having understood knowledge in this way, what do they understand as nirvāṇa?
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, they understand the Dharma itself."
Bhaiṣajyasena, for those who understand the Dharma in this very way and comprehend the compendium of the Dharma, the first gain arises;
by taking up what has been heard, there will be only a righteous gain.
[195] It is just as if, Bhaiṣajyasena, there were a certain man who was a merchant; while traveling for the sake of profit, he took a thousand man-loads of gold, both his own and belonging to others.
As he was going along, his mother and father said this to him: "Listen, noble son, these thousand man-loads of gold have been taken, both your own and belonging to others."

"You must handle this gold well; you must not let anything of it be lost. Having secured a great profit, ensure that the gold itself is well-secured, for that will bring us great profit and we shall live in comfort.
Then that son said to his parents, "I shall do so," and having spoken thus—
That merchant, having taken the gold, would depart; then, through negligence, that merchant might, within the span of a single month, destroy all the gold and bring it to ruin.
Then that man, overcome by supreme anxiety, his heart pierced by the arrow of grief, and filled with shame and modesty, would not enter his own home.
His parents, hearing that "all that gold has been destroyed by your son," would become hopeless, their hearts struck by the arrow of sorrow, and [would tear] their garments...

As he tore his clothes, lamented, wailed, and thus bewailed himself, [he thought]: "A wicked son has been born in our house in the form of a son; he has destroyed the entire household and, leaving us destitute, has reduced us to the status of slaves and laborers. His parents, their hearts overcome with anxiety and devoid of hope, passed away. Then that son heard that his parents had passed away, hopeless.
That son also passed away in utter despair.
In this very same way, Bhaiṣajyasena, the Tathāgata speaks this meaning:
those beings who do not have faith in my teaching pass away at the time of death having become hopeless, their hearts struck by the arrow of grief, and excluded from the great jewel of the Dharma.

Just as those two parents, hopeless, grieve and lament for the sake of gold, their hearts struck by the thorns of sorrow, overcome by the grief-thorn regarding gold that belongs to others or to themselves, and fallen into anxiety— [198] even so, Bhaiṣajyasena, those who do not have faith in my teaching later, at the time of death, experience painful sensations while burning with remorse and lamenting.
Having exhausted the merits previously performed, they no longer perform other merits directed toward a fertile field.

There, at that time and on that occasion, seeing those whose merit was exhausted and whose hearts were pierced by the arrows of grief, undergoing a terrible and dreadful rebirth in the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama, it occurs to them at the very moment of death:
"Who might be my protector, so that I may not [fall into] hell?"
"May I not see the realm of animals, hungry ghosts, or the world of Yama, nor may I experience that painful sensation.
As he was thus lamenting and departing for the next world, his parents spoke to him in this way: "What shall we do, dear son? And they addressed him with these verses:
(54) This disease, this suffering, this great terror cannot be grasped;
you shall not die, my son, for one who is ill fears death.
(55) You shall be liberated from this disease, which is so terrifying and fearsome.
"Maintain your fortitude, my son; from that, success will come.
The son said:
"My consciousness is obstructed and my body is being severely tormented."
All my limbs ache; I see my own death approaching.
(57) My two eyes do not see, and my two ears do not hear;
furthermore, I shall not regain my hearing, and this body will no longer endure.
(58) "My limbs ache as if they were senseless pieces of wood; O Mother, you are deceiving me, for death has not yet come to you. The mother said:
(59) "You ought not to speak thus, my son; do not cause me such terror. You see these afflictions in your body, which is overcome by fever.
The son said:
(60) I do not perceive a fever in the body, nor disease, nor does it suffer;
yet I see the terrible death and my body is utterly struck down.
(61) I see with my own self that the entire body is oppressed by suffering.
"To whom shall I go for refuge? Who will be my protector?
(62) His mother and father said, "Son, there must indeed be an appeasement of the gods' wrath. By performing a sacrifice to the gods, you will then attain well-being."
The sons said:
"You yourselves must do that by which my well-being may be secured;
go very quickly, indeed, and ask Devapālaka."
[200] Then his parents, having gone to the temple of the god, caused incense to be offered to the god.
Thereupon, that temple-keeper, having offered incense to the god, spoke these words:
"The god is angry with you; you must perform service for the god; a sacrifice must be performed."
"In that case, an animal must be sacrificed and a man must be sacrificed; then your son will be delivered from the disease.
Then, at that very moment, the parents thought: "What shall we do? We are poor.
If the King does not show favor, our son will die."
"Alternatively, if he would grant us his favor, we, being utterly destitute, shall bring him a beast and a man.

Then the two of them, having gone very quickly to their own home, sold whatever household goods were available there; they went for the purpose of purchasing a beast. At that time, they spoke thus to a certain man: "O man, give us the gold we have requested, so that we may be able to return it again on the tenth day."
"If we are unable to give that back to you, then we shall become your slaves and laborers. Then those two, having taken that gold, would go to buy an animal and a man;
and once they had bought an animal and a man, that man would not know that they intended to deprive him of his life.
Then those two parents, having fallen into a state of delusion, would no longer enter their own home.
Having gone to the temple, the two of them addressed the temple-keeper:
"Perform the sacrifice immediately!
Then the parents themselves caused that animal to be slaughtered and deprived that man of his life; thereafter, that temple-keeper began to prepare the fat for the sacrifice.
Then that deity descended and spoke thus:
"Your son has been accepted by me.
Thereupon, the parents, overflowing with joy and gladness, said: "It is better that our son lives; we shall become his servants."
Then, having turned back those parents and having performed a proper sacrifice for the deity, they went to their own home; there they saw that their son had passed away.
Thereupon, with hearts pierced by the arrow of grief through great suffering and despondency, those two parents became hopeless and died right then and there.
"In the same way, Bhaiṣajyasena, the association with non-virtuous friends is to be viewed.
He said: "I ask, Blessed One; I ask, Sugata."
He said, "Ask, Bhaiṣajyasena.
He asked, "Blessed One, where is the rebirth of those beings? What is their future destiny?
He replied, "Enough, Bhaiṣajyasena; what is the use of your asking about this matter?"
He said: "I ask, Blessed One; I ask, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
"In that regard, Bhaiṣajyasena, his mother has been reborn in the great hell Raurava."

The father was reborn in the Saṃghāta great hell; the son was reborn in the Tapana great hell; Devapālaka was reborn in the Mahāvici great hell. He asked: "Blessed One, where is a man who is innocent reborn? What is his future destiny? The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Bhaiṣajyasena, it should be understood that the rebirth of an innocent man is among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, in their state of companionship."
He asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, that this man was reborn in the company of the Trāyastriṃśa gods?

The Blessed One said: "Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena. At the time of his death, as he was being deprived of life, that man conceived a mind of faith toward the Tathāgata and spoke these words once: 'Homage to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha!'"
Bhaiṣajyasena, by that root of merit, he will experience the happiness of the Trāyastriṃśa gods for sixty kalpas;
for eighty kalpas he will remember his births from birth to birth;
and in every birth he will be free from all sorrow.
"From the very moment of birth, he will extinguish all sufferings.
Indeed, it is not possible to lead all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa.

When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, why is it not possible to lead all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa? The Blessed One—
He said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, vigor must be initiated.
[Bhaiṣajyasena] asked: "Lord, what is the initiation of vigor?
The Blessed One said:
Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena, the manifestation of fruits is called vigor;
namely, that which is called the fruit of stream-entry is a station of vigor,
and that which is called the fruit of once-returning is a station of vigor.
The fruit of non-returning is called a station of vigor;
the fruit of arhatship and the cessation of an arhat are called a station of vigor;
the fruit of a pratyekabuddha and the knowledge of the fruit of a pratyekabuddha are called a station of vigor.
The fruit of the bodhisattva stages is the station of awakening, known as the station of vigor.
These, Bhaiṣajyasena, are the names of the stations of vigor.
He asked: "Blessed One, how is the stream-enterer to be shown, and what is the fruit of stream-entry?"
The Blessed One said:
"Bhaiṣajyasena, it is just as if some man were to plant a tree;
on that very same day, a sprout would grow from the planted tree."
On the very day that a sprout has grown, on that same day it would sink one yojana deep;
and suppose another man were to plant a tree in exactly the same way.
Then, on that very day, due to the agitation of the wind, no sprouts of that tree would grow, and that man would uproot the tree from that spot—whereas another man [would act otherwise].
"Why do you dig up my land? he asked, engaging in quarreling, scolding, strife, and dispute.

At that time and on that occasion, the king heard that two men had become involved in mutual quarreling, scolding, strife, and dispute, and were arguing with one another. Thereupon, the king dispatched a messenger to them, saying:
"Go, my good man, and bring those two men here."
"So be it, Your Majesty," that man replied to the king. Taking leave of him, he hurried away and approached those two men, saying to them: "The king summons you both.

At that very moment, one of the men there was terrified and trembling, while the second man was neither afraid nor trembling; they were led before the king and stationed in his presence. Then the king spoke to them in this way:
"What is this, sirs? How has this quarrel, dispute, conflict, and contention arisen between you two?
Then those two men stood up and said this to the king: "Listen, Great King; we possess no land of our own.
On borrowed ground a tree was planted; on the very day it was planted, on that same day sprouts, leaves, flowers, and fruits appeared—half raw and half ripe."
And by this second man, on that very same day and in that very spot of earth, a tree was planted; yet,
no sprouts grew from that tree.
Because of the wind being agitated, neither leaves, nor flowers, nor fruits have appeared.
Furthermore, Great King, its root does not go even a yojana beneath the ground.
This man disputes with me, claiming it is your fault.
"Moreover, O King, you yourself should examine this and know for certain; there is no fault whatsoever on my part in this matter.
Then that king summoned thirty koṭis of ministers, assembled them together, and spoke thus: "Tell me, what do you say?"
The ministers said, "What shall we say,
Great King? The king said, "Where have you seen or heard of such a thing, that on the very day a tree is planted, on that same day a sprout grows, and leaves, flowers, and fruits are produced?"
"O you who are half-pregnant with the fetus of ignorance, you must reach this conclusion.
Then those ministers rose from their seats and said to the king: "Great King, it does not befit us to make this decision; nor shall we be able to state a conclusion regarding this matter.
Great King, this is a matter of wonder; first, this very man should be questioned: 'Speak, O man, is this matter true that you declare?'"
He said: "It is true, Great King, that this matter is so. The king said:
(64) "I have neither heard nor do I believe such hard-to-accept words as these from you."
"On the very day the tree was planted, on that same day it sprouted;
you say that on that very day it gave leaves, flowers, and fruit. With palms joined in reverence, that man then spoke to the king.
(66ab) Go yourself and plant the tree; see whether it sprouts a shoot.
[210] Then that king, together with thirty koṭis of ministers, went out;
he had those two men placed under arrest in prison.
Thereafter, the king himself planted the tree.
And that tree did not produce sprouts, nor leaves, nor flowers, nor fruits.
Then the king, being enraged, spoke thus:
"Go, sirs, and quickly bring axes for felling wood!"

When he had brought them, that man cut down the tree which he had planted, even as it appeared with leaves, flowers, and fruit. Out of anger he cut down that single tree, and twelve trees appeared; when those twelve trees were cut down, twenty-four trees appeared—made of the seven precious gems, complete with roots, leaves, fruits, and sprouts.
Then, from those twenty-four trees, twenty-four birds— cocks— manifested,
with golden crests and golden beaks, and feathers made of the seven precious gems.
Thereupon, the king, overcome by rage, took an axe in his own hand and struck that tree.
And from that tree, having been struck, nectar-water flowed forth.
Then the king, with a troubled mind, gave the command:
"Go and release those two men from their imprisonment in the prison-house. "So be it, Your Majesty," they replied.
At that very moment, the two men ran forth, released them from their imprisonment in the jail, and led them to where that tree was.
Then the king asked:

"Why is it that this tree, planted by you, being cut down as one, grew back doubled in size until it reached twenty-four branches, whereas the tree planted by me has produced neither sprouts nor leaves?"
He gave neither flowers nor fruits;
then that man spoke thus:
"O Great King, such merits as mine do not exist in you."

[213] Then those thirty million ministers, placing both their knees upon the ground before that man, spoke thus: "You must exercise the sovereignty; this former king is no longer fit. Then that man replied to those ministers in verses:
(66cd) I have no need for royal power or enjoyments, nor for grain or wealth;
(67) may I have grace from the Buddhas, that I may become the supreme among bipeds.
For the Tathāgata would indeed go to the peaceful realm of nirvāṇa,
where he might teach you the Dharma that leads to the city of nirvāṇa.
Then, having assumed the cross-legged posture, he made this vow:
"Whatever evil I previously committed has brought me to this imprisonment by the king;
but by making this aspiration, may my evil be destroyed."
[214] Then indeed, those twenty-four koṭis of birds and cocks struck the musical instruments with their diamond-beaks.
Then, at that time and on that occasion, thirty-two thousand gabled pavilions appeared.
Each individual gabled pavilion manifested with a measurement of twenty-five yojanas, and within each gabled pavilion, twenty-five birds— cocks— appeared,
with golden crests, golden beaks, and golden faces.
They uttered human speech:
"It was not well done by you, O Great King, that this tree was cut down;
for another twenty-four hundred million trees have now appeared."
"By this evil deed, you shall experience an undesirable fruit.
You do not know what kind of being it was by whom this tree was planted.
The king said:
"I do not know this matter; please explain it clearly, O Great Ascetic! What kind of being was he, by whom this tree was planted?
Thus spoke the birds.
(73) For this Leader, the illuminator of the world, shall arise as the liberator of all beings from the bonds of existence within saṃsāra.
The king said:
(74) "Which is the second being whose tree does not grow? Or what evil deed was committed by him? Tell me, O twice-born ones."
The birds said:
"Devadatta is indeed a fool, for the tree does not grow upon him.
Since he has performed no wholesome deed whatsoever, how can a tree grow for him?"

[214] Then, at that time and on that occasion, thirty koṭis of ministers, having heard this Dharma-discourse, all became Bodhisattvas established in the ten stages (daśabhūmi) and attained the superknowledges (abhijñā);
and that king also became established in the ten stages and attained the realization of wholesome dharmas (kuśaladharma-abhisamaya).

[215] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, that thirty million people have become established on the ten stages and have attained the supernormal powers?
The Blessed One said: "Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena; I shall explain it to you."

Then, at that moment, the Blessed One manifested a smile. Immediately at that time, from the Blessed One’s mouth, eighty-four hundred thousand rays of light issued forth— of many colors, various colors, and hundreds of thousands of diverse colors,
such as blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, crystal, and silver.

Having illuminated those infinite and boundless world-systems, they returned once more, circumambulated the Blessed One three times to the right, and vanished into the crown of the Blessed One’s head. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena rose from his seat, draped his robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and [turned] toward the Blessed One.

The Blessed One, having extended his joined palms toward him, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for manifesting this smile? Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or without condition.
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, do you see the multitude of people coming from all directions throughout the world-system to my presence?"
He replied, "No indeed, Blessed One, I do not see it.
The Blessed One said, "In that case, Bhaiṣajyasena, look and behold the multitude of people!
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, having looked, saw in the eastern direction a single tree that had appeared, measuring seven thousand yojanas in size; there, in one place—
Twenty-five thousand koṭis of people gathered together;

they did not speak, nor did they chatter, nor address one another, nor converse, nor eat, nor stand up, nor walk about, but remained accepting [the situation] in silence. In the southern direction, a single tree appeared measuring seven thousand yojanas, where twenty-five thousand koṭis of people gathered together.
They did not chatter, nor did they converse, nor did they engage in friendly talk; they did not speak, nor did they stand up, nor did they walk about;
they remained accepting the situation through silence.
In the western direction, a single tree appeared, measuring seven thousand yojanas in size; there, twenty-five thousand koṭis of people gathered.
They did not speak, nor did they converse, nor did they chat;
they did not utter words, nor did they stand up, nor did they walk about.
They consented by remaining silent.
In the northern direction, a single tree appeared, measuring seven thousand yojanas in size; there, twenty-five thousand koṭis of people had gathered.
They did not speak, nor did they converse, nor did they chat, nor did they utter a word, nor did they stand up.

They did not walk about; they remained patient in silence. In the upward direction, a single tree appeared, measuring seven thousand yojanas in size, where twenty-five thousand koṭis of people had gathered.
They did not speak, nor did they converse, nor did they chat, nor did they utter a word.

They did not rise, nor did they walk about; they remained patient in silence. To the lower direction, a tree appeared measuring seven thousand yojanas, and there a multitude of people numbering twenty-five thousand koṭis gathered.
They did not chatter, nor did they converse, nor did they speak, nor did they utter words; they did not rise, nor did they walk back and forth;
they remained patient in silence.

[218] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One: "I would like to ask the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, about a certain matter, if the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity to have my question answered. When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena: "Ask, Bhaiṣajyasena, whatever you desire; I shall answer each and every one of those questions for you."
"I shall satisfy their minds by answering what they have asked.

When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, why is it that these multitudes of people have come and are stationed throughout the world-systems of the four directions—indeed, from below up to the zenith, fifty koṭis of people have come and are stationed there—and yet they neither address nor converse with the Blessed One?"
They do not chatter, they do not speak, they do not discourse; they do not rise, nor do they walk about;
they accept [the situation] through silence.
“Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition? The Blessed One said: “Go yourself, Bhaiṣajyasena, and ask those Tathāgatas from which world-system these multitudes of people have come.
He asked: “By whose power of supernatural might, Blessed One, shall I go?”
"Is it by the power of the Tathāgata’s supernatural might, or by your own supernatural power?
The Blessed One said, "Go, Bhaiṣajyasena, by means of the empowerment of your own supernatural strength;
then return again by the power of the Tathāgata’s supernatural might."

[220] Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times to the right, vanished right there. Then, having passed beyond ninety-six koṭis of world-systems from this world-system, there is a world-system named Candrapradīpa; there, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Candrāvatikṣetra currently resides, stays, and maintains his life.
Surrounded and honored by a retinue of eighty thousand *koṭīs* of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, he was teaching the Dharma.
Then the bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasena arrived at that world-system.

Thereupon, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena approached the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, [and Perfectly Enlightened One] Candrāvatikṣetra. Having approached, he [stood before] that Blessed One...

Having bowed his head at the feet of the Perfectly Enlightened One and standing before him, he extended his joined palms toward where the Blessed One was and addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, having traversed ninety-six thousand millions of world-systems from the Sahā world-system, the Buddha-field of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, I have come here; yet, Blessed One, I have never seen so many beings anywhere else."

"Whatever was seen there— what, Blessed One, is the cause and what is the condition that a great multitude of people has gathered before the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, in the Sahā world-system, having come from the ten directions,
and while standing there I see them, yet being here I do not see them?"
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, they move about and dwell right there. He asked:
"But how is that so, Blessed One?"
The Blessed One said: "Sentient beings are produced from insentient trees.
He asked: "Blessed One, by whom has this been seen, and by whom has it been heard, that humans are born from an insentient tree?
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, you have not seen [or]..."
"Nor have I heard that humans are born from an insentient tree.
He replied, "O Blessed One, neither have I seen nor have I heard that humans are born from an insentient tree."
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, do you wish to see it? I shall show it to you right now. He replied: "I wish to see it, Blessed One; I wish to see it, Sugata.
Then, at that moment, the Tathāgata Candrāvatikṣetra extended his own arm, which was adorned with a hundred merits.
Then, from his arm, hundreds of thousands of millions of hosts of people appeared; and each host of people, extending a hundred arms, showered the Tathāgata with various perfumes and ointments.
Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Candrāvatikṣetra, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena:
"Do you see, Bhaiṣajyasena, this host of people showering the Tathāgata with various perfumes, garlands, and ointments?"
He said, "I see them, Blessed One; I see them, Sugata.
The Blessed One said, "These mindless multitudes of people have appeared; these mindless humans have been reborn."
Then, indeed, the hundreds of arms belonging to each one of those hundreds of thousands of millions were all cast off.

[224] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, having seen this, said this to the Blessed One: "What is this, Blessed One? What is this, Sugata, that in a mere moment the hundreds of arms of these humans have been cast off? If, Blessed One, even those with a hundred arms are not released, what need is there to mention whether humans with only two arms will be released?"
The Blessed One said: "In this very way, Bhaiṣajyasena, beings are born without consciousness; they cease without consciousness.
Bhaiṣajyasena, our own body also should be regarded as having become devoid of consciousness."
He asked: "Blessed One, which beings are young, and which are old?
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, there are beings who are young, and there are those who are old.
He asked: "Blessed One, which are the young, and which are the old?"
He said, "Those that are currently scattered are the old ones; those that have emerged from the trees are the young ones.
He said, "I wish, Blessed One, to see the young beings.
Then, indeed, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Candrāvatikṣetra, extended his right palm.
Then, from the ten directions, hundreds of thousands of millions of multitudes of people arrived. From the direction below and the direction above, fifty million multitudes of people arrived.
Having arrived, those multitudes of people bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One; yet they did not address the Tathāgata nor converse with him, but remained silent and waited in reverence.

[226] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, why is it that these beings do not address the Tathāgata, do not converse with him, but instead remain silent?
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, you do not understand; the ground is insentient, and thus they do not address or converse with him.
It does not cognize the aggregate of Dharma."
For what reason? Bhaiṣajyasena, there are some young beings here who do not know arising and do not know cessation.

Having seen neither old age, nor sickness, nor sorrow, nor lamentation, nor separation from the beloved, nor union with the unloved, nor being deprived of the beloved, nor death, nor untimely death—and having seen none of those all-pungent sufferings—they do not apply themselves to effort; how then shall they come to know?
"Bhaiṣajyasena, you must instruct them again and again.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, from where do these young beings come? From where do they pass away?"
Where are those reborn who do not know (or understand) the Dharma? The Blessed One said: "Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena, as to the human form they assume."
That was not made by a silversmith,
nor was it made by a weaver,
nor was it made by a carpenter.
It was not made by a potter;
it does not arise out of fear of a king.
Through the union of male and female, it comes into being conjoined with sinful karma.
Again and again they cause those beings to learn various crafts,
yet an endless and bitter suffering arises for them;
there they experience the ripening of their previously committed evil karmas through those bitter sensations.
"Bhaiṣajyasena, it is right here that these young beings have come who do not speak, do not converse, and do not rise, as they experience such painful sensations.
For this reason, Bhaiṣajyasena, they do not speak and do not converse."
In this way, Bhaiṣajyasena, those young beings, being ignorant of what is wholesome, do not know arising and do not know cessation;
nor will they obtain a human existence.
These, Bhaiṣajyasena, are called "young beings."

[228] He asked: "Blessed One, how do young beings arise? How do they cease? The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, it is just as if some man were to rub wood with wood to produce fire; gradually that wood would be set ablaze by the fire.
In the very same way, Bhaiṣajyasena, the human body first comes into being."
And being born, he experiences sensation.
He asked: "Who, then, is truly born? Who is truly passed into parinirvāṇa?
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, only a Buddha is truly born; only a Tathāgata is truly passed into parinirvāṇa."

[229] It is just as if, Bhaiṣajyasena, a man had been cast into confinement and imprisonment by a king in a certain dark house, a chamber of gloom. Having entered that dark house, the man would see the interior of the house, a place of total darkness. Then another man, having seen him, might think because of his own past experiences of suffering: "This man is lost; unpracticed in life, he will go to destruction through suffering."
Having brought fire there, he would cast a subtle flame into that inner chamber.
That man, confined in the prison, would see the ray of fire; having seen it, he would become comforted and his courage would increase. Then, for some reason, that fire would burst into flames;
by that blazing fire, the house would be set ablaze on all sides, and that man would be burned right there. When the king heard that he had been burned, he would fall into anxiety and distress.
It would occur to him: "I shall no longer subject any being in my own realm to confinement in prison.
Then that king would thus reassure those beings dwelling in his realm: "Do not fear, O beings; do not be terrified!
Let there be fearlessness for you; there shall be no further application of punishment in my realm."
There will be neither imprisonment nor confinement;
nor shall I cause the loss of life for any sentient being.
O beings, may you be free from fear.
In the same way, Bhaiṣajyasena, the Tathāgata has burned away all afflictions and pacified all diseases; yet, just as that man burned his own body because of the house fire,
he remains engaged for the sake, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings.

Just as one would liberate beings from execution, bondage, and imprisonment, even so the Tathāgata— having abandoned the stains of passion, hatred, and delusion— has arisen in the world like a lamp for all beings and liberates them from the realms of hell,
animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras;
he liberates both young and old beings.
[231] Then, at that very moment, these verses issued forth from the sky above:

(76) Oh, what a field! The field of the Victor, a well-prepared and excellent field, wherein seeds once sown never come to ruin. (77) The Buddha-field is the field of the Victor; the teaching of the Victor is highly praised.
The Teacher indeed employs skillful means for the sake of gathering all sentient beings;
though established in the realm of nirvāṇa, he appears upon the surface of the earth.
Having brought peace to the entire world, the Buddha purifies the sacrificial offerings.
(79) He liberates new beings and he liberates those who are ancient;
having liberated all beings from the three realms in successive order,
(80) the gates of hell are indeed closed, and the animals and hungry ghosts are set free.
For peace has been established in this world, and happiness has been secured in the next world.
[232] Then, at that moment, the Blessed One manifested a smile and said:
(81) “Excellent is the sight of the virtuous Buddhas; excellent is their vision. Excellent is the quality of the Dharma, the field, and the sight of the harmony of the Saṅgha.”
(82) "Excellent! Those who shall hear this sūtra, this instruction on the *Saṃghāṭa*, which destroys all evil, will attain the unsurpassed state.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, having extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what is the cause? What is the condition?"
In order to manifest a smile, the Blessed One said:
"Son of good family, do you see these young beings?
He replied: "I see them, Blessed One; I see them, Sugata."
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, all these will this very day become bodhisattvas established on the ten stages."

[234] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena stood eighty thousand yojanas above in the sky. Thereupon, eighty thousand koṭis of sons of gods rained down a shower of flowers over the Blessed One. And those young beings, having seen this, all joined their palms in reverence and paid homage.
[235] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, while remaining in the sky, spoke these words:
By means of which he fills the triple-thousand great-thousand world system with sound;
the beings born in the thirty-two great hells hear that sound,
and the thirty-two classes of gods also hear that sound.

The triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system shook in six ways, and eighty-four thousand dragon kings in the great ocean were agitated. Thirty thousand billion *rākṣasa*s came to this Jambūdvīpa;
twenty-five thousand billion *preta*s, *yakṣa*s, and *rākṣasa*s gathered at the royal capital of Aḍakavatī, and a great assembly was formed before the Blessed One.
[236] Then the Blessed One taught the Dharma to those young beings.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of world-systems in the ten directions arrived by means of their respective supernatural powers.

Then the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, having extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "O Blessed One, O Sugata, there are many, many bodhisattvas..."
They had assembled and were seated; O Blessed One, many gods and nāgas had also assembled and were seated.
Furthermore, numerous rākṣasas and pretas had come to the royal capital of Aḍakavatī and had assembled and were seated in order to hear the Dharma.
[237] Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena: "Come, son of good family!

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, descending from above by means of his supernatural power, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One and said this to the Blessed One: "The Aggregate of Dharma..."
"Regarding the term 'aggregate of Dharma' (*dharmaskandha*):
Blessed One, by how much is it said that one is called an 'aggregate of Dharma'?
The Blessed One replied: 'Noble son, regarding the term "aggregate of Dharma," it is said as follows.'"
He who seeks the holy life, having sought the holy life, desists from all evil.
Do you see, noble son, these young beings who desist from unchastity?
He replied: "I see them, Blessed One; I see them, Sugata."
He said: "They will surely have attained the *dhāraṇīs* and will be endowed with all dharmas.
He asked: "By what means, Blessed One, have so many beings gathered together?"
Then, in order to hear the *Dharmaskandha*,
the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena:
"Bhaiṣajyasena, there are many sentient beings."
Those who do not hear that birth itself is suffering; those who do not hear that old age itself is suffering;
those who do not hear that illness itself is suffering.

Sorrow and suffering, the suffering of lamentation, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the suffering of association with the unbeloved—death removes all these sufferings. Bhaiṣajyasena, this body and life are called "all-suffering.
Then, having heard this teaching, those young beings extended their joined palms toward where the Blessed One was and said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, we too must die."
The Blessed One said: "Noble sons, you too, as well as all sentient beings, must die.
They asked: "Blessed One, how does the time of death arrive?"

The Blessed One said: "O sons of good family, at the time of death, within the final consciousness, there is the wind called 'the cessation of consciousness,' the wind called 'the delusion of consciousness,' and the wind called 'endowed with the agitation of consciousness. O sons of good family, these three winds, at the moment of death, churn the final consciousness, cause it to be agitated, and produce agitation."
They asked: "Blessed One, what are the three that strike down the body at the time of death when consciousness is ceasing?
The Blessed One said: "O worthy ones, they are called Śastraka, Sūcaka, and Ṣṭhīlaka;
these are the ones that strike down the body."
He asked: "What, Blessed One, is this thing called 'body'?
The Blessed One replied: "Friends, it is called 'blazing,' it is called 'an abode of burning,' and it is called 'a heap of filth.'"
And one named Śṛṅgārika;
and one named Śmaśānika; and one named Durbuddhika.
It is called "heavy with burden"; it is called "oppressed by birth";
and it is called "agitated by birth."
That which is called "the nourisher of life" and that which is called "the bringer of death and separation from the beloved"—
these, friends, are what are termed "bodies."
They said: "How, Blessed One, does one die? How does one live?
The Blessed One replied: "Venerable ones, that which is called consciousness dies; venerable ones, that which is called merit lives."
"Friends, what is called the body dies; it is bound by millions of sinews, bound by eighty-four thousand veins and capillaries, and bound by twelve thousand limbs.

It is bound by three hundred and sixty bones, and within it dwell eighty-four thousand families of worms. Death occurs for all those living beings, and the cessation of death also occurs there; at that point, all those living beings become hopeless."
When that person dies, then a violent agitation of the winds among all living beings arises for the purpose of devouring one another; at that time, they experience painful sensations.
Some, moreover, grieve for their sons;
others grieve for their daughters or their kinsmen. All of them, pierced by the thorn of sorrow, begin to devour one another.
They all, in turn, devoured one another until only two living beings remained. Those two fought for seven days, and when the seven days had passed, one of the living beings was crushed.
One is liberated.

What, venerable ones, is called "Dharma"? What do you think? Just as all living beings die through the mutual cessation of one another, even so do foolish, ordinary beings encounter mutual destruction.
They do not fear birth;
they do not fear diseases;
they do not fear death, just as those two [did].

Two living beings are fighting; in this very same way, foolish ordinary people fight with one another. Then, at the time of death, they are addressed by virtuous men: "O man, why do you place your trust [in this world]?
Have you not seen any misfortune whatsoever in the human realm?"
"The danger of birth has not been seen; the danger of old age has not been seen; the danger of illness has not been seen; the danger of death has not been seen.
He replied, "Venerable sirs, the danger of birth has been seen by me; the danger of old age has been seen; the danger of illness has been seen; and finally, the danger of death has been seen."

He said: "How is it that you have not performed those roots of merit which ought to be performed? Why, O man, have you not cultivated the roots of merit consisting of the aggregates of Dharma, which bring about welfare in both worlds?
Friends, I ask you a second time."

"Why have you not accumulated the equipment of roots of merit, by which you might be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death? Why have you not performed the investigation through wise attention?
O man, have you heard the sound of the gong being struck upon the earth?"

Furthermore, you have not seen the humans of Jambudvīpa giving gifts, performing meritorious deeds, observing the fast, or planting seeds of roots of virtue in the field of the Tathāgata—whether by offering incense, garlands, or lamps; nor have you seen edible or consumable food being given, nor have you seen the four assemblies of the Tathāgata being satiated, or the monks...
Whether it be a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā who has entered these four assemblies within the Teaching, they speak and address him with such beneficial words:
"O man, nothing at all was done by the gods; rather, something evil was committed by you after coming to this Jambudvīpa.
When he has died, the King of Dharma at that time, instructing that man, speaks these verses:
(83) Having seen the appearance of a Tathāgata, having heard the striking of the ghaṇṭā,
and having heard him teaching the Dharma— peaceful and leading to Nirvāṇa—
(84) why have you not performed merit that brings happiness in the next world?
"You shall experience suffering in hell, the fruit of your undesirable karma.
Then that man replied to the King of Dharma with these verses:
"I was of childish intellect, following the influence of evil friends."
An evil deed was committed by me with a mind deluded by desire;
and because that desire was cultivated by me, its terrible fruit has now arrived.
I have indeed caused harm to living beings and destroyed what belongs to the Saṅgha.
[87] I have committed the desecration of a stūpa with a corrupted and malevolent mind;
I have uttered wicked speech, and my mother was tormented. [88] I recognize the offense that was committed by my own body.
I see my rebirth in the most dreadful Raurava hell; likewise, I shall experience the sensation of suffering in Saṃghāta and Pratāpana,
and I shall undergo bitter sensations in Mahāvīci.
(90) And in the Mahāpadma hell, I shall wail, deeply afflicted;
for a hundred times I shall be born in the Kālasūtra hell, which is full of great terror.
(91) Even when the beings in the hells have been struck down, they see that fear once again.
Furthermore, they shall undergo a hundred yojanas of great terror;
scorched within the Kumbha hell, they will not find an exit again.
Moreover, there is a hell named Kṣura, extending for a thousand [yojanas] and filled with razors.
A hundred thousand times ten million razors arise before him;
by means of those, his body is pierced due to his own evil deeds.
[94] Violent winds, most terrible, shall tear asunder that entire body;
such sufferings must certainly be experienced by me in hell.
[95] All sentient beings shall behold my body tormented by pain.
For the sake of building this house, I have taken wealth belonging to others;
likewise, my sons, daughters, brother, sister,
as well as my mother, father, and the circle of my friends and kinsmen.

(97) I have wandered through various evil deeds involving slaves, laborers, cattle, servants, and livestock, as well as with vessels of silver and gold. (98) Likewise, I have wandered while having houses constructed with very fine garments.
Having constructed a most wonderful house, crowded with men and women,
and having struck the lutes and musical instruments, my mind— difficult to subdue—
delights; yet even now, that grateful one has not anointed his body with scented waters.
(100) You are a body devoid of consciousness; I have been deluded because of you.
There is no being whatsoever who could be my protector or knowledge for me.
(101) Amidst the most terrible agitation of the winds and the torment of the body—

Various delicious flavors were tasted by the tongue; likewise, many beautiful, variegated garlands were bound upon the head. The eye was beguiled by such beauty, and no protection for the eye exists. (102)

(103) "The eyes of the wicked were the cause for what was done by me upon seeing them; my ears were likewise the cause, and my arms were struck down like thunderbolts. (104) Bracelets were bound upon my hands, and rings upon my fingers."
Around his neck were pearl necklaces, and his feet were well-adorned;
having fashioned lattice-work right there, he stood upon a golden pedestal.
Furthermore, his limbs were set with various jewels, as were his golden bracelets.
(106) Though I have enjoyed vast pleasures that gladden the mind, and have indulged in my tender touch, I was seized by craving.
(107) My body has been entertained with various spreads and beds;
it has been bathed in clear perfumed waters and anointed with fragrant unguents.
(108) It has been fumigated with divine camphor, sandalwood, and incenses.

A garment treated with musk was made to enhance its color; it was perfumed with *gandhavārṣika* oil and with *sumanā*, *caṇpaka*, and other flowers, and this pale-colored cloth, fine as Kāśī silk, was put on.
(110) Having descended from the back of an elephant and mounted the back of a horse,
I think, "I am the king," and people run before me.
(111) I consider myself well-trained in song and dance within the inner apartments.
"Deer were slain by me with arrows during the hunt though they were innocent.
Such was the sin committed by me, ignorant of the next world;
I ate the flesh of others, and therefore this suffering is mine."
(113) "Death was not known to me; it will come as something terrible.
I was of childish intellect, and my body was nourished by me.
(114) Death has arrived for me today; no protector whatsoever is found."
For you are all my kinsmen; why do you gaze at my face?
(115) Why do you tear your clothes, and for what reason these lamentations? Why do you dishevel your hair? What can blood possibly accomplish?
(116) Why do you throw dust upon your heads and beat your breasts? I am not to be deterred from living; what is the use of your weeping?
(117) My body is the food for wolves, dogs, and crows.
This body, nourished in vain by birds,
will become like one touched by the serpent of death;
therefore, one should employ medicine in such a way that one is liberated from this fear.
(119) Whatever medicine the physicians may give me is not desired by me now; rather, I desire the medicine of the Dharma, which liberates one from the serpents of the afflictions.
(120) It must be given to me while I am dying; do not offer this [other medicine] to me!
This body, which must inevitably perish despite being nourished—
why do I project this mass of evil that will later yield only suffering?
This beloved body, once nurtured by me, will act with ingratitude.

(122) "O sons and daughter, why do you stare at me with your eyes? Save me from this disease; why do you weep so pointlessly? For you, my sons and daughter, have now become ungrateful toward me. (123)
I have taken what belongs to others for the sake of supporting you.
Now that I have met my death, why do you leave me without hope? I am terrified by the miserable states of rebirth and tormented by this death.
(125) Sensation, perception, mental formations, contact, and supreme sensations—
the fool is led astray by craving and reaps a bitter fruit;
(126) for me, born into an adverse family, there is the great bond of sorrow.
But knowing me to be one of little merit, other people will grieve for me; fallen away from generosity and morality, and turned away from the Dharma,
I do not understand rebirth, being afflicted by the venom of the serpent of the afflictions.
(128) The fool is deluded by ignorance where liberation does not exist;
being confused, he does not understand the purpose of liberation and commits evil deeds.
(129) The fool, whose mind is constantly distracted, is perpetually deluded by the afflictions.
For this body, bound by various fetters, is consumed by blazing fire; bewildered, the body wanders where no happiness is found,
and it does not know that happiness which brings ultimate bliss.

The field of the Buddhas bestows happiness; it is the wheel of Dharma, the great medicine, and the morality and truth of those who observe discipline—the Tathāgatas whose voice is like that of Brahmā.
