[244] Then the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena and said this: "And so it is, Bhaiṣajyasena, that beings lament at the time of death. Indeed, there will be no savior for them other than the ripening of the fruit of their well-performed deeds. And he spoke these verses:
Having committed evil deeds, they indeed fall into the hells; there they consume glowing embers and drink molten iron.
Embers rain down upon their bodies, and being scorched, they cry out most piteously.
In this most terrifying hell, their bodies are consumed by fire;
they do not recognize pleasures, nor do they understand the Dharma.
The fool wanders about through unrighteousness and attains no pleasure whatsoever.
(135) Endowed with faith and virtue, possessed of wisdom, and performing great austerities,
one who associates with virtuous friends will quickly become a Tathāgata.
(136) One exerts vigor for the sake of what is excellent, in order to be reborn in the world of the Buddhas.
"Teach the wholesome Dharma that embraces all sentient beings;
having entered into a mind of loving-kindness and being devoted to the holy life,
Bhaiṣajyasena, upon hearing this, you should become intent on its practice."
(138) That which is called the awakening that perceives liberation, the leader of pleasant sound, the mother and father of the world— that is the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
(139) It is the supreme spiritual friend who teaches what is extremely difficult to perform.
In this world of Dharma, those who listen to the teaching of the Buddha with reverence shall become Buddhas, Sugatas, the supreme among men;
they shall become Protectors of the World, the liberators of all sentient beings. (140)
Those who possess reverence for the peaceful Buddha-fields.
(245) Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, why does this earth tremble and shake so violently?
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena: "Look, Bhaiṣajyasena; what do you see?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena looked.
Then, at that very moment, he sees from the four directions;
the earth opens up,
and as the earth is opened, he sees.
From the fissures of the earth, twenty koṭis of humans are born;
in the downward direction, twenty koṭis of humans are born;
and in the upward direction, twenty-five koṭis of humans are born.
[246] Then those young beings, having looked upon the Blessed One, said this to him: "Blessed One, who are those born here?
The Blessed One said: "Do you see these multitudes of people?
They replied: "We see them, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said, "These groups of people have become your friends.
They replied, "Blessed One, will death also come to these beings?
The Blessed One said, "It is so, friends; death will come to all beings as well."

[247] Then those former beings who were young and had been born earliest, having extended their joined palms toward where the Blessed One was, said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, we are not able to behold birth and death again. The Blessed One said: "In that case, do you have the courage to obtain the power of vigor? They replied: "We would wish to see the Tathāgata face to face and [to hear] his..."

"May we hear from his presence the Dharma—sweet and pleasing—and may we behold the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples seated there; may we behold the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power and great majesty. O Blessed One, we do not venture to see such birth and death. Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, by the power of his supernatural faculties, rose from his seat along with those five hundred Bodhisattvas; they all rose by means of their supernatural powers into the sky above.
They walk back and forth,
and having assumed the cross-legged posture, they meditate;
from all their bodies, lions emerge.
Tigers come forth;
venomous serpents come forth;
elephants come forth.
They display great miraculous transformations;
they sit upon mountains having assumed the cross-legged posture;
and they ascend twenty thousand yojanas into the air.
Ten thousand times ten million moons and suns descended.

Then those young beings said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for this great radiance of rays and this great miraculous display of supernatural power in the world?
The Blessed One said: "Noble sons, behold these two, the moon and the sun, who have appeared."
They said, "We see it, Bhadanta Bhagavat; we see it, Bhadanta Sugata.

The Bhagavat said, "This radiance from their own bodies and this miraculous display of supernatural power have been shown by the Bodhisattvas; having displayed them, they teach the Dharma to sentient beings."

For the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings—both gods and humans—they have displayed the power of vigor and manifested such power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*) even within this very human body. He said: "May the Blessed One teach the Dharma for the manifestation of the radiance of light rays."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena: “Bhaiṣajyasena, do you see this trichiliocosm shaking in six ways?
“I see it, Blessed One; I see it, Sugata.
“Blessed One, it occurred to me: ‘I should ask the Tathāgata about this matter.’”

The Blessed One said: "Ask, Bhaiṣajyasena, whatever you desire; I shall satisfy your mind by answering each and every question, I shall explain, analyze, and, Bhaiṣajyasena, I shall reveal all that pertains to the past, future, and present times. He said: "May the Blessed One teach me for the sake of dispelling remorse."
"Here, Blessed One, I see the Tathāgata surrounded by eighty-four thousand sons of gods, surrounded by eighty-four thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas,
surrounded by twelve thousand koṭis of nāga kings,
surrounded by eighteen thousand koṭis of bhūtas, and surrounded by twenty-five thousand koṭis of pretas and piśācas."

The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, these beings who have gathered and are seated here in this assembly to hear the Dharma from me—Bhaiṣajyasena, they shall turn their backs on saṃsāra this very day; they shall become attainers of the ten stages this very day."
Established on the ten stages, they will attain the realm of nirvāṇa.

Seeking the welfare of all beings, having performed the Dharma for the sake of liberating them from old age and death, and bringing about happiness, they will conquer the snare of the afflictions and attain the teaching of the Buddha.
He asked: "Blessed One, have these beings arisen through many stations of beings by means of various and diverse karmas?"
They stood surrounding the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said: "Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena! He replied:
(141) "Deluded beings do not know from where liberation will come."
Many new beings will today attain dhāraṇī;
they shall know all dharmas for the sake of attaining the ten stages,
and having attained those ten stages, they will perform the work of a Buddha.
(143) They shall turn the wheel of Dharma and rain down the rain of Dharma; my teaching is delightful, for by it sentient beings have gathered—
(144) gods, nāgas, pretas, and even the most formidable asuras.
Established upon the ten stages, having struck down [all things] with the sound of the Dharma,
sounding the drum of the Dharma and filling the conch of the Dharma—
today, this shall become the power of vigor for these nine beings.
(146) Today these beings shall attain the Dharma just as it was attained by the Tathāgatas.

[252] Then, about five thousand young beings rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows: “Blessed One, this body is a heavy burden and a terrible source of great fear;
by means of it we are bound in saṃsāra, remaining ignorant of its end.”
(148) We do not recognize the path, for the path itself is not seen. O Protector, we have become like the blind; please take us under your care.
(149) We entreat you, O Hero: teach the Dharma, O Leader!
We were born with little wisdom and are indeed ignorant of happiness; teach us the Dharma!
Deliver us from this terrible suffering.
Wherever we may be reborn, may there be for us the vision of the Buddha.

[253] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena approached those young beings; having approached them, he addressed those young beings with a verse: "Eat your food, drink this wonderful juice, and afterwards, having become confident, you shall hear the Dharma without fear."
They said:
"Venerable Elder, who are you? We do not know you.
We see that you are gracious, of peaceful appearance, and of great renown."
(153) You have been liberated from the great terrors of hell, the animal realm, and the world of hungry ghosts; all your sins are pacified, so that you shine resplendent in the world.
(154) We see in your hand a water-pot endowed with the seven precious gems.
The Sūtra, consisting of jewels, was wrapped around your body, which was a mass of splendor;
we were not able to carry it away. We have no need for food, nor for delicious drink. (155) Your words are peaceful.
(156) From food, excrement arises, and likewise urine from drink;
blood comes from the essence (*rasa*), and from blood, flesh is produced.
(157) We have no need for food, nor even for well-prepared drink.
Their garments shall not be fine, nor made of silk or fine cotton;
their bracelets shall not be of gold, nor shall they wear ornaments of pearl;
they shall not wear rings on their fingers, for all of them are perpetual observers of dharma.
(159) We seek only our lives and would not go to an evil rebirth; we seek the gift of Dharma, not even the pleasures of the gods.
(160) One should cultivate the state of a spiritual friend, not the sovereignty of universal monarchs.
The universal monarchs will die, leaving behind their most beautiful continents;
neither sons, nor wives, nor daughters follow after them,
and even the seven treasures do not turn back, nor do they go along behind.
(162) Having assembled a great multitude, they do not turn their backs, nor do they run ahead; they no longer remain under [his] control.
(163) Kings who have been born only once have been led astray by this constant [delusion].
Having committed sinful deeds, they fall into the Raurava hell.
Having traveled in all four directions with the seven great and powerful jewels,
where will that supernatural power go when one dwells in Raurava?
(165) Having died, they are unable to attain supernatural power where no ground exists;
O Elder, listen to us: go where the Tathāgata is.
(166) We long for a vision of him, just as a mother and father do for their child.
We have no mother, no father, and no brothers;
the Tathāgata alone is the teacher of the world, our mother and our father,
and he is both the moon and the sun who reveals the path of security.

(168) For he is the liberator from saṃsāra, by whom one is not born again; he is the non-ferryman across the flood, the great terror of the flood of afflictions. (169) By him sentient beings have been ferried across, never to return again.
The True Dharma was taught by him for the sake of supreme enlightenment;
we have no need for food, nor do we desire the fruits of kingship, nor is it our purpose to go to the world of the gods, for we are terrified of the hells.
(171) A human birth is seen to be pleasant where the All-Knowing One appears,
yet those with short lifespans are seen due to their own evil deeds.
(172) They are attached to sensual enjoyments and do not perceive death.
They do not know and they do not fear, being devoid of [understanding] cessation and arising;
they do not know subtle phenomena and they do not perform subtle deeds.
With minds overcome by ignorance, they do not know the peaceful realm.
(174) Passing away, they do not grow weary, yet they are born again and again;
for a long night, struck by suffering, they are constantly beaten with rods.
(175) They will seize what belongs to others, and likewise they are slain and bound.
Bound by the five fetters and impelled by their former sins, they will die devoid of hope, pierced by the thorns of grief;
as their consciousness is being obstructed, they lament piteously.
(177) Who indeed might be my protector? I shall give away all my possessions—gold, silver, and crystal—and I shall even become a slave.
(178) I will perform every task that is worthy of a servant.
"I have no need for the enjoyments of kingship, nor for grain or wealth.
(179) I have need only of my own body; one who commits evil is never released.
Thus, O Elder, there would be no food for us."
(180) Even kings will die, though they have enjoyed exquisite food;
even sons of gods will die, though they have drunk the most excellent drink, (181) that refined food and drink endowed with various flavors.
Having brought it before him, the king touches the food with his tongue;
for kings, greedy for flavors, commit no small amount of evil. They take delight in transient tastes wherein no essence is found.

(183) We must not drink, nor indeed must we eat; such is the nature of reality that we must practice, so that we may be liberated from suffering. (184) [It is] the liberation from the bond of craving, the release from the affliction of craving.

We have gone for refuge to that Buddha who is liberated from all bonds. Indeed, we go for refuge to the Great Seer, the Lord of the World; we go to pay homage to him whose appearance is dear to all beings. (185)
(186) "We do not know your name; tell us your auspicious name.
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasena said:
"Indeed, you all wish to hear the name of every person."
(187) Surrounded by nine hundred thousand crores of beings, the Tathāgata was addressed as follows:
"We wish to hear your name, which arises from all virtues.
(188) "Your name is heard to be profound; you are a disciple of the Buddhas. He replied:
"I am Bhaiṣajyasena by name; indeed, I am the medicine for sentient beings. I shall teach you all the supreme medicine, which pacifies every disease, for people afflicted by every ailment."
(190) Passion is a disease, a great disease that perishes dreadfully in the world;
delusion is a most terrible disease by which the unwise are made to wander. (191) Sentient beings indeed go to hell, as well as to the realms of animals and hungry ghosts.
These fools are seized by hatred; how can there be peace for them?
They said:
(192) "Having heard this auspicious Dharma, may we be liberated from all suffering;
yet, though liberated from all sufferings, we were of childish intellect and ignorant."
Free from evil deeds, we shall hear the gift of Dharma; having abandoned all evil, with fear and terror utterly destroyed,
we shall quickly behold the Perfectly Awakened One, the liberator from all diseases.
To the King of Physicians, the Great Physician, the healer of those who suffer—
(195) go quickly, O Elder, to pay homage to the Tathāgata.
And in our name, pay homage and speak thus to the Guide of the World:
(196) Quench this disease, quench this most terrible fire!
For this entire body is ablaze, and though it is being consumed, it is not extinguished.
(197) O you of noble vows, show compassion toward us who are afflicted by suffering.
The burden of the body is a great burden, a sharp burden, and most terrible;
overcome by hatred and delusion, people always carry it.
Again and again these ignorant ones carry it, yet they do not carry the burden of liberation.
(199) They do not realize they must die, and thus no fear arises in them.
Not knowing the path to liberation and not seeing the path to liberation, (200) they remain complacent, thinking, "Death shall never come to us."
Agitated, they do not recognize it; even while seeing their mother, they perceive her as dead.
Others do not remember their father, and being constantly tormented by disease and agitated by afflictions and karma, how can they eat food?
(202) We do not understand the end of suffering; we labor in vain.
Such sufferings as ours arise from birth and have ignorance as their cause.
(203) [There is] great terror and a heavy burden: perception, mental formations, and feeling.
The fool who does not understand the Dharma is led astray by craving.
Born indeed for the sake of misfortune in this world, encumbered by the burden of the body, he thinks:
"I must perform bathing and anointing; I must have clean clothes that are very beautiful."

(205) One should prepare refined food that is pleasing to the body, and likewise request from others the delightful sound of the five musical instruments for the ear. (206) When the seven precious jewels appear, the eyes become attached to their form.
The tongue craves every kind of savory and delicious taste;
the body always longs for soft and subtle touch;
and pleasure arises when the two fleshly parts of the body press against one another.

(208) For this body is indeed insentient; who could find delight in it? My feet find pleasure there because they are covered with beautiful leather. (209) Neither clothing nor ointments provide protection against death.
The body would not be a protection; how much less so clothing and ointments?

(210) A person is said to be the body; it possesses breath, great strength, and sharp power. One should apply discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) toward that [body] as having great qualities within the physical frame.
(211) Formerly, surrounded by horses and elephants, I was made to wander about in sport; ignorant of the dharma of liberation, I took delight in sinful deeds.
(212) Out of a desire for play, and unaware of the next world, I caused sin to be committed.

Again and again I was born, and again and again I met with death; again and again sorrow was seen, along with the bonds of lamentation. The death of mothers was witnessed, and fathers dead were seen as well.
(214) Kinsmen, sisters, sons, and even a wife who has died—all conditioned phenomena are indeed empty. For what conscious person would take delight in them?
(215) Indeed, with a mind seized by greed, I believed in trust.
I did not perceive the peaceful Dharma, nor did I rejoice in death. Therefore, with a mind shrouded by greed, I gave no gift.
What evil could be equal to greed, which even today does not desist?
(217) We have indeed become bewildered, and the entire world is bewildered;
bewildered, we hear a sound concerning the adoption of false doctrines. (218) We seek liberation and meditations, yet we do not sustain our bodies.
May we become Buddhas for the sake of the world, teachers and gurus in the universe. The Buddha is the mother and father in the world; the Buddha is the one who reveals the path.
He rains down the rain of Dharma everywhere throughout Jambudvīpa.
(220) Deluded beings do not know how the gathering of dharmas occurs;
by directing the mind toward awakening, the gathering of dharmas is attained.
(221) All conditioned phenomena are empty; enjoyments as well as wealth are likewise empty.
Seeing ourselves as empty, we have become despondent. O Elder Bhaiṣajyasena, listen to our words:
we would distance ourselves from you for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
(223) The Bodhisattvas, possessing vigor and great austerity, do not grow weary; remembering the faults of saṃsāra, they practice the gathering of virtues.
(224) Go to where that Teacher is and ask on our behalf.
The Teacher, having attained bliss, the Jina, is not at all weary;
Māra, along with his army and his mounts, has been defeated by you.
You have swiftly kindled the Dharma that brings happiness to all sentient beings.
(226) Nor have we heard the Dharma by which we might become Buddhas. Go quickly, O Elder, for the sake of our welfare!
(227) We shall not cross over as long as we do not see the Tathāgata.
All stood there with reverence, beholding him who bore the thirty-two marks of a great man.
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasena said:
"Look upward for now; what do you see at this moment?
They looked upward and saw five [Bodhisattvas] standing there, no fewer than that.
Three hundred thousand gabled pavilions were on all sides,
constructed from the seven precious gems and beautifully adorned with nets of jewels;
in their center was a fully blossomed lotus, emitting divine fragrances.
(231) There they asked the Elder, "What is this that is seen here— these peaked pavilions with jeweled lattices, resting upon the filaments of lotuses?
Bhaiṣajyasena said:
(232) These are your stations; go to behold the Buddha!
Pay homage to that World-Illuminator, who is the transcendent Teacher.
They said: "In that regard, we do not know and do not see the path [to] the Tathāgata;
since we do not know the path, where shall we go to pay him homage?"
Bhaiṣajyasena said:
"One must go to pay homage to the Teacher, whose radiance is like nectar;
he cannot be grasped, being like infinite space."
(235) This Teacher stands firm, just as the Merus stand;
he is like Sumeru, and his depth is like that of the great ocean.
And because of the arising of the Buddha’s wisdom, there is no dust even in a trichiliocosm.
The Illuminator of the World was honored by Bodhisattvas in the ten directions.
They said:
"Look upon us, O Lord of the World; fulfill our aspiration! The Teacher has been saluted by us with our hearts, and from that we have obtained the fruit."
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasena said:
"The Teacher is not attached to perfumes, nor to garlands, nor to ointments;
he grasps the cause for sentient beings by which they are liberated from the conditioned."

(239) Māra shall not wage a most dreadful battle against him who has tamed his mind and gone for refuge to the Buddha. (240) He shall not fall under the power of death and will swiftly attain the dhāraṇī.
Having produced clarity of mind, he then beheld the Teacher.
Then indeed the Blessed One, the Tathāgata whose voice is as pleasant as the song of the kalaviṅka bird, manifested a smile.

Then indeed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, rising from his seat and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "O Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason..."
The sign for the manifestation of his smile was that eighty-four hundred thousand rays of light issued forth from the Blessed One’s mouth;
by those rays, this great trichiliocosm was filled with radiance, all thirty-two great hells were suffused with light, and the thirty-two celestial palaces were illuminated.

And those rays were of various colors—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, crystal-colored, and silver-colored. These rays, having issued from the Blessed One’s mouth, performed every service for the comfort of sentient beings throughout the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system; then, returning once more, they circumambulated the Blessed One seven times to the right and vanished into the crown of the Blessed One’s head.

[255] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One: "I would like to ask the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, about a certain matter, if the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity to have my question answered."

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena: "Ask, Bhaiṣajyasena, whatever you desire; I shall satisfy your mind by answering each and every question you ask.
When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena spoke thus to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, thirty thousand koṭis of new beings have appeared."
They do not penetrate the subtle teaching of the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
O Blessed One, they revile, disparage, and oppress the elders among sentient beings, saying:
"You elders do not understand the Dharma; you are always attached to what is non-Dharma and unwholesome."
“Lord, they speak words that are refined and pleasing; for what reason do they speak to the Blessed One in such a way?
The Blessed One said: “Bhaiṣajyasena, you do not know for what reason these beings speak in this way.
Having heard the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata—gentle and pleasant—they will, because of that, Bhaiṣajyasena, realize the meaning of all dharmas and become endowed with all virtuous qualities.”
They shall come to be;
and all shall penetrate the dhāraṇīs.
From this day forward, they shall be established upon the ten stages.
Today they will sound the great drum;
today they will become endowed with the great methods of the Dharma.
Do you see these peaked pavilions, Bhaiṣajyasena?
Bhaiṣajyasena said, “I see them, Blessed One; I see them, Sugata.
The Blessed One said, “Today, Bhaiṣajyasena, these young beings, having ascended into these gabled palaces, will attain the realization of the Dharma.
Today they will bring all wholesome qualities to complete fulfillment.”
Today they shall beat the great drum of the Dharma.
Today there will be a realization of the Dharma for many hosts of gods.
And for many beings who have set out toward the states of woe in the hells, upon hearing this teaching of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, there will be a complete turning away from and defeat of all saṃsāra.
And at that time, ninety-nine billion elder beings will all attain the fruit of stream-entry, and they shall be endowed with all dharmas.
Bhaiṣajyasena, they shall all be completely freed from all suffering.
Bhaiṣajyasena, all of them will accomplish the vision of all the Tathāgatas.
Bhaiṣajyasena, all of them will be endowed with the Great Dharma.
Look around in the four directions, Bhaiṣajyasena!

[258] The bodhisattva mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena looked all around in the four directions. He saw that from the eastern direction fifty koṭis of bodhisattvas, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, were coming;
from the southern direction sixty koṭis of bodhisattvas, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, were coming;
and from the western direction seventy koṭis of bodhisattvas, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, were coming.
From the northern direction, eighty *koṭis* of bodhisattvas, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, arrive.

From the downward direction, nine thousand *koṭis* of bodhisattvas, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, arrive. From the upward direction, one hundred thousand *koṭis* of bodhisattvas, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, arrive.

Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who had arrived, having approached the Blessed One and bowed their heads at his feet, stood to one side. Then, while those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who had come from the ten directions were standing to one side, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is this black form and red form that I see in the sky, in the atmosphere?"
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, what is this?
Do you not recognize that black form and red form which you see in the sky?
He replied: "I do not know, Blessed One; I do not know, Sugata."
The Blessed One said: "Only the Tathāgata knows this.

Bhaiṣajyasena, this Māra has approached here for the purpose of causing [the Bodhisattvas] to lose their sight. "Bhaiṣajyasena, do you wish to see these Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas who are stationed there in the midst of the sky?
He replied: "I wish to see them, Blessed One; I wish to see them, Sugata."
[260] Then the Blessed One, having shown those bodhisattvas, addressed the bodhisattva mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena:
"Bhaiṣajyasena, hundreds of millions of bodhisattvas, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, have arrived who are just like these.
He asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, that so many bodhisattvas have come here?"
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, by reason of these young beings, all beings will now become endowed with the meditation on the Dharma.
Do you see, Bhaiṣajyasena, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas of various forms who have arrived through the empowerment of their supernatural power?

He replied: "I have beheld world-systems as numerous as the sands of a hundred billion Ganges rivers; therein I have seen bodhisattva mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges rivers."
Each abides by means of their own respective power of supernatural transformation; they abide in various forms, various colors, and various strengths and configurations.
Those bodhisattvas abide in the dwellings of the noble Dharma;
those retinues of bodhisattvas abide in the dwellings of the Dharma.

[260] Thus spoke the Blessed One. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas—both new and old—and the entire assembly, including the world of gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
Colophon B:
The Great Vehicle Sūtra entitled *Saṃghāṭa*, a great discourse on the Dharma. [End.
Colophon D:
The Noble Discourse on the Dharma entitled *Saṃghāṭa* is completed. [End. [End.]
